Jan Olof Jonson (born 11 January 1962) is a Swedish electrical engineer whose work argues that the whole of electromagnetism can be derived from Coulomb's law alone, once retardation and the special theory of relativity are applied consistently, and that Maxwell's field theory is therefore unnecessary.
Education

Work
Jonson has contributed to Natural Philosophy Alliance and CNPS conferences continuously since 2000, and the programme running through that body of work is a single one. His starting point is the standard observation that the magnetic force between currents is the electrostatic force seen from a moving frame — the derivation familiar from Purcell's textbook — and his claim is that if this is carried through rigorously, with the propagation delay of the interaction taken into account element by element, Coulomb's law by itself accounts for the forces between conductors, for electromagnetic induction and for radiation, with no independent magnetic field required.
The recurring test case is Ampère's bridge , a rectangular circuit divided into two halves that repel one another. This experiment sits at the centre of a two-hundred-year-old dispute over whether the force between current elements takes Ampère's original form, which includes a longitudinal component, or the Grassmann form underlying the modern Lorentz force . He is one of the most substantial figures catalogued on this wiki. He published more than two hundred papers, sat on the editorial board of Physics Letters A , and was known in the French press as l'hérétique de la physique and l'éternel résistant — the second a reference to his wartime service in the French Resistance as much as to his standing in physics.
For this wiki his most directly relevant contribution is a specific one: the argument that a small but non-zero photon mass makes the small ether drift measured by Michelson and by Miller not an embarrassment to relativity but a consequence of it.

Vigier earned his Ph.D. in Mathematics from the University of Geneva in 1946 and served briefly as a member of the French Atomic Commission alongside Frédéric Joliot-Curie. Jean-Claude Pecker (10 May 1923 – 20 February 2020) was a French astrophysicist, author and rationalist. He was Professor at the Collège de France from 1964 to 1988 and Director of the Institut d'Astrophysique from 1972 to 1979, and served as General Secretary of the International Astronomical Union from 1967 to 1970 and as Secretary of the International Academy of Humanism. He wrote several books and hundreds of papers on astronomy, astrophysics, cosmology, human rights, pseudoscience, science and society, and the history of astronomy.
His principal research was in solar physics and stellar atmospheres — the textbook Astrophysique Générale , written with Évry Schatzman, was a standard reference for a generation — and it is from that established position that he engaged, from the 1980s onward, with objections to the standard cosmological model.
Cosmological work
Pecker's contribution to the non-standard cosmology literature centres on the redshift . With Jean-Pierre Vigier he developed a tired-light mechanism in which the redshift arises from an interaction between photons carrying a small non-zero rest mass and the matter lying between source and observer, an account set out in " A Possible Tired-Light Mechanism " (1988). He also worked with Toivo Jaakkola on spatial fluctuations in the Hubble constant, and set out his objections to the standard model directly in " Some Critiques of the Big Bang Cosmology " (1997).

He argues that the "worst theoretical prediction in the history of physics" — the roughly 120-order-of-magnitude mismatch between the observed cosmological constant and the vacuum energy density predicted by quantum field theory — is not a physical puzzle at all but the symptom of a notational and geometrical mistake buried in the way physics represents energy density and the constituents of a line. Baugher was affiliated with the Department of Electrical Engineering at Wright State University in Dayton, Ohio, at the time of his 2013 paper in Progress in Physics . Earlier he co-authored engineering work with Ronald A. Coutu on micromechanical structures with stable linear positive and negative stiffness, published in the Society for Experimental Mechanics conference series ( MEMS and Nanotechnology , Volume 4, 2011). Jeffrey Joseph Wolynski (born December 3, 1984) is an American independent researcher and self-published author known for developing and promoting the General Theory of Stellar Metamorphosis , a hypothesis proposing that stars gradually cool and evolve into planets. He is a prolific writer on the subject, having released several hundred short papers through open preprint repositories. His ideas fall outside mainstream astronomy and have not been published in peer-reviewed scientific journals or adopted by professional astronomers.
Biography
Wolynski is American and resides in Cocoa, Florida. Beginning around 2012, he began publishing a series of papers outlining what he calls stellar metamorphosis, circulating his work largely through preprint archives such as viXra , the General Science Journal, and personal websites and video channels rather than through established academic journals. He is affiliated with the Natural Philosophy Alliance community of independent researchers, under which he describes his work as that of a "Scientific Revolutionary." Jesse Babcock (born 1915) is an American self-taught theorist associated with the Natural Philosophy community. He is known for an unorthodox cosmological framework he calls the "true suction" theory, which he developed to explain the origin of matter, energy and Gravity outside the framework of mainstream physics.
Biography
Babcock reports having only an eighth-grade formal education, a fact he presents as central to his outlook, arguing that it left him unencumbered by conventional scientific training. By his own account he became interested in perpetual motion as a child before 1923, and at around the age of fifteen concluded that a working perpetual-motion device could not be built until "the secret of the universe" was understood. He states that experiments imagining spring-and-spoke wheel mechanisms convinced him that any purely mechanical arrangement will always balance out, ruling out perpetual motion in practice.
Babcock dates the origin of his theory to 1953. He recounts hearing a radio report that high-frequency sound waves from jet engines were damaging the lungs of ground crews, which led him to reconsider the idea that sound is "nothing." Reflecting on empty space, he concluded that space must be endless and that it is the only source from which anything could arise.

Babcock's central claim is that space itself possesses a dynamic characteristic he terms "true suction," from which all matter and energy originate. In his view "true suction" is not an object or substance but a property of space, and everything that exists ultimately derives from space and this characteristic.

Work
The Essential Guide grew out of a request made in 2009 by David Talbott to Bob Johnson, for a summary that would give newcomers enough grounding in plasma behaviour to follow Electric Universe arguments without finding them far-fetched. He presented the project at the 18th Natural Philosophy Alliance conference in 2011, in a paper whose interest lies less in its physics than in its frankness about the state of the field it serves. Johnson describes the Electric Universe as a "paradigm" rather than a theory, on the grounds that its ideas "are less than full-blown theory and are still in a very qualitative state of patterns and examples", and that "underlying mathematics is not yet the EU's long suit". He defends that status as a legitimate stage of enquiry by appeal to the qualitative-physics literature in artificial intelligence, particularly Johan de Kleer's work on causal reasoning about circuits, and argues that the task ahead is to deepen the model with quantitative work rather than to defend it as complete.

John B. Miller is an American physicist and astronomer associated with Western Michigan University in Kalamazoo, Michigan. With his collaborator Thomas E Miller he developed the de Sitter redshift interpretation of the redshifts of quasars and galaxies — an account in which cosmological redshift is a gravitational effect of de Sitter spacetime rather than evidence of an expanding universe.
Scientific work
Miller's work addresses one of the puzzles that has long fuelled non-standard views of redshift : quasars at very high redshift appear almost as bright as objects at intermediate redshift, which is difficult to reconcile with the expansion interpretation, in which more distant (higher-redshift) objects should generally appear fainter.
In his 1994 paper " Are Quasars Manifesting a de Sitter Redshift? " Miller proposed that quasar redshifts are a de Sitter redshift — a gravitational redshift arising in de Sitter spacetime, whose asymptotic character causes the redshift to rise very steeply with distance. On this interpretation an object's observed redshift is not a simple measure of recession velocity or distance, and the near-constant apparent brightness of quasars across a wide range of redshifts becomes expected rather than anomalous.
With Thomas E Miller he later extended the analysis to large modern surveys, arguing that under a de Sitter-space interpretation the intrinsic brightness of objects is roughly the same at all redshifts — for instance, that some 95% of Sloan Digital Sky Survey galaxies and quasars fall within a magnitude range of only about 2.8. The John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society ( CNPS ) is a worldwide society of critical thinkers — professors, PhDs, scientists, engineers and interested lay people — who openly question mainstream physics and cosmology and who develop and present alternative theories, philosophies and models. Taking "natural philosophy" in its older and broadest sense, the society covers physics, cosmology, mathematics and the philosophy and history of science, and provides an open forum for serious scientific work that falls outside the accepted paradigm. It is the organization that owns and maintains the Natural Philosophy Wiki on which this article appears, together with the associated World Science Database.
The society describes itself as "a world-wide think-tank of critical thinkers... who openly criticize mainstream physics and cosmology and who propose alternative theory, philosophy, and models." Its members — many of whom have worked together for more than two decades — apply critical thinking to identify what they see as flaws and failures in mainstream science, and to propose new directions in natural philosophy.
Namesake
The society is named in honour of Dr. John E. Chappell Jr. (1933–2002), a historian of science and earth scientist widely regarded as the modern father of the organized "dissident science" movement. Chappell founded the Natural Philosophy Alliance , the CNPS's predecessor, and devoted much of his life to promoting open, scholarly debate of alternatives to accepted physics — motivated in large part by his conviction that Einstein's theory of relativity was mistaken. Like Pierre-Marie Robitaille , Hartnett is a case of dissent issuing from technical accomplishment rather than from outside the discipline. His work on ultra-stable cryogenic oscillators is mainstream precision metrology of a high order, commercialised and sold to national standards laboratories. His cosmology is not accepted at all.

Hartnett was born in Manjimup, Western Australia. He took both his B.Sc. He worked for many years in the Frequency Standards and Metrology research group at UWA, latterly as a research professor, and subsequently at the University of Adelaide. He has published more than eighty papers in refereed journals and holds two patents.
Frequency standards and metrology
Hartnett's experimental speciality is the cryogenic sapphire oscillator — a frequency standard in which a pure sapphire resonator, cooled with liquid helium, supports an exceptionally stable microwave "whispering gallery" mode. Hunter is a British researcher in cosmology and gravitation who proposes that the observed expansion of the universe is better understood as a global rescaling of all lengths and physical constants, and that dark energy is an artefact of misreading the relationship between redshift and scale factor.
Work
The rescaling symmetry principle
Hunter's central proposal, set out in " The Rescaling Symmetry Principle " (2008), is that every length in the universe and every physical constant changes continuously and simultaneously, at a rate governed by the number of length dimensions in the quantity concerned: d Q / Q = aH d t , with H half the Hubble constant. Lengths and the speed of light carry a = 1, Planck's constant 2, the gravitational constant 3, the permittivity of free space −3, while masses, the fine structure constant and the Hubble constant are unchanged.
Because everything changes together, he argues, no local experiment can detect the change — timing light over a fixed distance, or lunar laser ranging for a drift in G , must both return null results. The cosmological redshift, on this account, arises from the changing value of Planck's constant rather than from expanding space.
He reports that the resulting magnitude–redshift relation matches the Type Ia supernova data without invoking dark energy, and that a matter density of one quarter critical follows naturally, with an equation of state parameter of −1.

His own summary of the position, given in the World Science Database record below, is that "dark energy is an illusion created due to the misunderstanding of the relationship between redshift and scale-factor", and that the model reproduces the WMAP5 value of Ω m = 0.249. John J. Durie is an author known within the dissident-science community for his paper on the telescopic aberration of light, a phenomenon central to long-running disputes over the aether and Einstein's special relativity . He is listed in Jean de Climont's Worldwide List of Dissident Scientists .
Biography
Little verifiable biographical information about John J. Durie is available. He is documented primarily through his 1983 paper on stellar aberration and through his inclusion in de Climont's Worldwide List of Dissident Scientists . His work was circulated within critical-physics circles; the archived copy of his paper was contributed by the dissident physicist Thomas E. Phipps Jr.
Scientific work
Durie's known contribution is his paper "On the Telescopic Aberration of Light," published in the Toth-Maatian Review in January 1983. The paper addresses the aberration of starlight first reported by James Bradley in 1728, in which the observed direction of a star shifts with the Earth's orbital motion. This effect has long been treated as a test discriminating between an aether -based account of light propagation and the relativistic explanation. Durie's analysis engages the classic questions of stellar aberration and ether drag, placing his work among dissident treatments that revisit whether telescopic aberration truly favors special relativity over an aether model.

John O'Malley Bockris, an Australian electrochemist, coined the term "hydrogen economy" in the 1970s. Bockris' hydrogen economy describes a system in which hydrogen would be used to transport energy from renewable sources over large distances and store it in large amounts. In 1962, Bockris first proposed a plan to supply US cities with solar-derived energy via hydrogen. In 1971, he published the first article on hydrogen in a referred journal. Bockris (1923–2013) was one of the significant figures of twentieth-century electrochemistry, and the great majority of his work is entirely conventional. Born in Johannesburg and raised in England, he took his doctorate at Imperial College London, where he ran a research group in the late 1940s — Martin Fleischmann was among the graduate students who joined its discussions. He moved to the University of Pennsylvania in 1953, then to the Flinders University of South Australia, and to Texas A&M in 1978, where he held a Distinguished Professorship until his retirement in 1997.
His textbook Modern Electrochemistry , written with A. K. N. Reddy and first published in 1970, became one of the discipline's standard works and remains in print. He published several hundred papers across five decades on electrode kinetics, the structure of the electrical double layer, electrocatalysis, corrosion and fuel cells, and supervised a very large number of doctoral students.

Scientific career

John W. McAlister is an American consulting engineer based in Delray Beach, Florida, who has built table-top mechanical experiments intended to test the equivalence of gravitational and inertial mass.
Work
McAlister's first paper, " A Mechanical Test of the Equivalence Principle " (1992), reported an anomalous energy loss in a magnetically suspended body revolving inside a spinning centrifuge, the centrifuge providing a pseudo-gravitational field.
Its successor, " A Special-Case Test of Newton's Second Law of Motion " (2010), was designed to reproduce the effect in a simpler configuration whose retarding forces could be enumerated. A half-kilogram weight falls on a wire over a pulley, drawing a carriage of 1.0 to 4.5 kg along a marble runway on three roller bearings; a microsecond timer records the fall. From thousands of runs over six months he reports an "inertial force index" — the factor by which the carriage's inertia must be increased for the force balance to close — of between 1.030 and 1.118, and concludes that gravitational and inertial mass should not be treated as equal.
The paper's chief merit is that it publishes the full grid of results across eight carriage masses and four drop lengths rather than a single figure, which is what makes the systematics visible: the discrepancy grows as the carriage gets lighter and as the drop gets longer, neither of which a modification of Newton's second law could produce.
He presented the 2010 work at the 17th Natural Philosophy Alliance Conference .

García Juliá's central claim concerns the origin of the redshift observed in the light of distant galaxies. In place of the standard reading, on which the redshift measures the expansion of the universe, he argues for a tired light mechanism: photons lose energy gradually in transit through an exponential decay E ( t ) = E (0)e − t /τ , so that the Hubble constant is reinterpreted as the inverse of an energy-loss time constant rather than as a rate of expansion.

Light crossing intergalactic space interacts with the microwave background and acquires the cosmological redshift; light generated inside a quasar interacts with that object's much denser radio-wave field and acquires an intrinsic redshift on the way out. Joseph C. Lucas is an American physicist and independent researcher, and the author — with his father Charles W. Lucas, Jr. — of the physical geometrical packing model of the atom and nucleus that forms the atomic-structure component of the Common Sense Science programme.
His contribution is a specific and unusually concrete one. Taking Bergman 's toroidal ring electron as given, Lucas asked what happens when such objects — real, finite-sized rings of circulating charge, each carrying a magnetic dipole — are packed around a nucleus. Using combinatorial geometry constrained by results he obtained from physical experiments with ring magnets , he derived the sizes of the successive electron shells as 2, 8, 18 and 32 — the shell structure actually exhibited by the Periodic Table — together with an argument for why the table has exactly seven periods and no shell of 50. The same packing analysis was then applied to protons and neutrons, yielding the nuclear magic numbers and an account of nuclide spin.
He introduced the model in Galilean Electrodynamics in 1996, and it was reprinted and extended in the Common Sense Science quarterly Foundations of Science between 2002 and 2003.

title: Just Which Equivalence Principle Do You Believe In?
content_preview:
Title Just Which Equivalence Principle Do You Believe In?
Author(s) James Carter
Keywords Equivalence Principle
Published 1998
Abstract
The Pound-Rebka experiment is often presented as an experimental proof of the Equivalence Principle. However, careful examination of this experiment reveals five different ways that its results can be interpreted. While all are compatible with the Equivalence Principle. each offers a distinct view of both gravity and the nature of the photons being measured. As a result, the Equivalence Principle has a different meaning and definition fur each interpretation. After each of these five possibilities has been presented, the listeners will be asked the following questions for discussion. Does anyone have a different explanation of this experiment? Which Equivalence Principle do you believe in? Since only one of these explanations can be correct, does anyone know of an experimental method by which one of these could be shown to be superior over the others and thus established as the true reality?

5th (B) Natural Philosophy Alliance Conference (17 May 1998)

Karl Teppo (born 1928) is a Finnish-Australian writer on cosmology, living at Mermaid Waters in Queensland, who has published a series of papers since the 1980s on the origin of the elements. He describes himself as an amateur, and his papers are unpublished pieces circulated through the Natural Philosophy Alliance rather than journal articles.
His work is more coherent than the three separate titles below suggest: they are three applications of one idea.
Biography
Nothing is recorded about Teppo's education or working life; the World Science Database gives his occupation simply as "Retired". He attended the 18th Natural Philosophy Alliance Conference in 2011.

The neutron as the fundamental particle

Because a free neutron decays in about fifteen minutes into a proton, an electron and an antineutrino, he argues, physics has given "too much importance to the bits" and overlooked the neutron itself. His motivating observation is that the heavier elements of the periodic table contain substantially more neutrons than protons.
Top-down instead of bottom-up
From that he derives what he calls Top-Down element evolution, set against the standard account he attributes to Eddington, Bethe and Fred Hoyle, in which hydrogen fuses into heavier elements in stars and supernovae and matter accretes into stars and planets from cold clouds. title: Kennedy-Thorndike experiment
content_preview:
The Kennedy–Thorndike experiment was an interferometer test carried out by Roy J. Kennedy and Edward M. Thorndike and published in 1932, designed to detect a dependence of the speed of light on the velocity of the apparatus rather than on its orientation . It is the companion to the Michelson–Morley experiment , and the two together are what actually pin down the Lorentz transformation — a point that is easy to miss, and that a good deal of the argument catalogued on this wiki turns on.
What it did, and why the difference matters
The 1887 Michelson–Morley apparatus had two arms of equal length and was rotated. A rotation test asks whether light takes different times along different directions. If the arms are equal, an isotropic slowing of clocks in the moving frame cancels out of the comparison, so the experiment is sensitive to length contraction but blind to time dilation.
Kennedy and Thorndike therefore built an interferometer with arms of deliberately unequal length — differing by about 16 cm, the largest difference their light source's coherence would tolerate — and did not rotate it. Instead they left it fixed and photographed the fringe pattern over months, letting the Earth's rotation and its orbital motion change the instrument's velocity. Under the Lorentz–FitzGerald contraction hypothesis alone , with no time dilation, an unequal-arm interferometer's fringe pattern should shift as the speed of the apparatus changes. The apparatus was mounted in vacuum in a temperature-controlled bath, since with unequal arms a fraction of a degree of drift would swamp the effect. They found no shift attributable to the Earth's motion.
The logical structure was made explicit by H. P. Robertson in 1949 and refined by Mansouri and Sexl in 1977. Three classes of experiment are needed:
Michelson–Morley constrains the dependence of light speed on the direction of travel — length contraction.

title: Kepler's Second Law and Conservation of Angular Momentum
content_preview:
Title Kepler's Second Law and Conservation of Angular Momentum
Author(s) Pari Spolter
Keywords kepler, gravity, planets
Published 2011
Abstract
Kepler's second law is calculated for 18 planets and asteroids. It is shown that equal areas are swept in equal intervals of time only near the perihelion (P) and the aphelion (A). A highly significant relation between the ratio of the area swept at the average of P and A to the area swept at semimajor (S) in the same interval of time and the eccentricity is presented. The equation is ratio = a⋅eb+c with a = −0.617, b = 2, and c = 1.00. The correlation coefficient is 0.9975. The ratio is equal to (1 - e^2)^1/2 , which is equal to sin θ, where θ is the smaller angle between the two vectors v and r. Angular momentum is a vector perpendicular to the plane formed by v and r and is conserved, indicating that there is no torque in the direction vertical to the plane of the orbits.

Khan’s Open Challenge to Einstein’s Relativity was a live session presented by Roger J Anderton on 15 November 2025 in the John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society live session series.
Mohammad Shafiq Khan challenges the mainstream and presents a critique of relativity. Hosted by Roger Anderton.
Summary
Roger J Anderton took up the open challenge to Einstein's relativity posted online by Mohammad Shafiq Khan , an independent researcher with a master's in physics, and ran it past ChatGPT. Khan's central charge is that Einstein's 1905 paper rests on trickery: Voigt's transformation was a mathematical possibility, Lorentz altered it by introducing the gamma factor, and the result is a manipulation rather than a physical argument — so that nature was made subservient to mathematics, and relativity, the big bang and spacetime all descend from it. His papers appeared in the Indian Journal of Science and Technology in 2012 and as an open letter to physicists, and, as Anderton noted, were ignored regardless of having been published.
Right from a certain point of view
Asked flatly whether Khan is right, the assistant said no. Asked whether Khan is right from a certain point of view, it said yes — and that second answer was the talk. Anderton framed it, as he had before, with Obi-Wan Kenobi's "what I told you was true, from a certain point of view", offering it not as a defence of relative truth but as a diagnosis of what relativity has done to the idea of truth.
The concession, once drawn out, was fairly substantial. Khan's objections are conceptual rather than empirical: discomfort with the relativity of simultaneity, a preference for absolute time, and an objection to the derivation. "This booklet is a compilation exploring the history of kinetic gravitational theories in the very prolific period spanning the 18th and 19th Centuries. Natural philosophers before, during and after Isaac Newton attempted to determine the cause of gravitation without resorting to the mystical notion of "action-at-a-distance". Historians of science often state incorrectly that Newton's Principia (1687) leads to the idea that gravitational force can act across empty space without any medium between bodies. Lambda CDM Cosmology overview and Roundtable Discussion was a live session presented by Harry Hamlin Ricker on 21 September 2024 in the John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society live session series.
The Standard Cosmology known as Lambda CDM Cosmology will be presented and discussed in a roundtable format, where participants are invited to join in the discussions.
Summary
This was a survey rather than an argument: Harry Ricker set out what the standard cosmological model actually says, in the belief that one cannot criticise a theory whose vocabulary one does not share. He ran it as a roundtable, pausing after each section for comment, and much of the value is in the interruptions.
What the model is
Lambda-CDM — the concordance model, in Sabine Hossenfelder's phrase — is big-bang cosmology with two additions. Lambda is the cosmological constant, associated with the vacuum or dark energy, introduced to account for the expansion accelerating; CDM is cold dark matter, undetectable except through its gravitational effect on luminous matter. It assumes general relativity and an expanding metric space, a direction and universal scale for time, and the cosmological principle.
Ricker flagged his own difficulties as he went. What is meant by metric space is never made clear — to him it is an abstraction, an empty void, and what exactly is expanding is unexplained. He traced the model's shape through the diagrams: an initial flash, inflation by a factor of some 10 27 , a long coasting period during which galaxies form, and a late acceleration attributed to dark energy. His starting observation is that the equations of different branches of physics share a recurring shape which the separate notational conventions of each branch conceal — so that the same role is played by quantities with unrelated symbols, while one name may cover quantities playing different roles.
His scheme arranges every physical quantity on a matrix whose axes count powers of length and of time, so that neighbouring cells differ by one factor of a metre or a second. Quantities are then sorted into four domains — gravitic, thermic, electric and magnetic — alongside two special ones for space-time and for energy; into four groups according to whether they carry, promote or oppose the transfer of energy; and into generic roles — charge, current, flux, potential, field, resistivity, permittivity and so on — defined without reference to any particular domain.
The organising axiom is a single generalised form of Ohm's law: Effect = Cause / Opposition . Because roles are defined generically, the scheme implies quantities that are unfamiliar or unnamed in one domain but standard in another, such as a gravitic permittivity or a current of heat; Hollo notes that most of these already exist under other names. Abstract
Urbain Le Verrier became famous by discovering Neptune from its effect on the orbit of Uranus. He turned his attention to Mercury, publishing a preliminary paper in 1841 and a definitive paper in 1859 on the Theory of Mercury. He discovered an unexplained shift in the perihelion of Mercury, which he attributed to the presence of a small unknown planet he called Vulcan, which was never found. The results were corrected in 1895 by Simon Newcomb, who increased the anomalous shift by about 10% but offered no new explanation for it. Albert Einstein, at the end of his 1916 paper on General Relativity, derived a specific solution for the perihelion shift which exactly matched the discrepancy. Dating from the 1947 Clemence review paper, that explanation and precise value have remained to the present time, being completely accepted by theoretical physicists as absolutely true. The highly technical 1859 Le Verrier paper was written in French, and astronomers and theorists have gone on from the study of the Solar System to the study of the Universe. The partial translation given here throws light on Le Verrier's analysis and thought processes, and points out that the masses he used for Earth and Mercury are quite different from present day values, possibly leading to a different fit to the old data. A 1924 paper by a professor of Celestial Mechanics critiques both the Einstein and the Le Verrier analyses, and a 1993 paper gives a different and better fit to some of Le Verrier's data. Leslie C. Case (September 11, 1930 – July 15, 2010) was an American chemical engineer, inventor, and independent researcher who, in the later part of his career, became known within the Cold Fusion community for a gas-phase process he called "catalytic fusion."
Biography
Case was born in Tulsa, Oklahoma, on September 11, 1930. He spent his career as a chemical engineer and inventor, holding patents in the field of polymer chemistry; his work on polyether polyols was the subject of the reported patent-office case Case v. CPC International, Inc. (U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, 1984). Case had a broad range of interests over his life, including gemstone cutting, the recovery of shale oil, the growing of grapes and production of wine in Australia, and alternative energy. He died at his home in Newfields, New Hampshire, on July 15, 2010, at the age of 79.
Education
Several degrees, including a Doctorate of Science — Massachusetts Institute of Technology
Work
In his later years Case turned to low-energy nuclear reaction research, which he preferred to describe as "catalytic fusion" rather than "cold fusion." His approach used a sealed container holding a precious-metal catalyst supported on activated carbon together with deuterium gas. In demonstrations he loaded activated carbon, including coconut-shell carbon, with roughly 0.1 to 0.5 percent by weight of a precious metal, reporting that palladium at about 0.4 percent worked best. When the sealed cell was pressurized with deuterium (on the order of a few atmospheres) and heated to roughly 200 °C, Case reported excess heat and the accumulation of helium-4, which he interpreted as a signature of deuterium-deuterium fusion.

Keywords light, photon, wave–particle duality, luminic motion, aether, propagation, aberration, Particle Model
Light is the most contested phenomenon in physics. Everyone agrees on what light does — it propagates in straight lines, refracts, diffracts, interferes, polarises, carries energy in discrete amounts, and travels at a definite and very large speed. What no one has satisfactorily explained is what light is , and what — if anything — it travels in .
This article is about the nature and propagation of light . Two closely related questions are treated at length elsewhere on this wiki and are only summarised here: the constant c and whether it is invariant is the subject of Speed of Light , and the quantum of light is the subject of Photon .
The literature collected on this wiki contains some 260 papers bearing on light. They do not agree with one another. They include corpuscular models in which light is literally made of particles, wave models in which it is a disturbance of a real medium, models in which it is neither and models in which it is both, entrained-aether accounts of its propagation, ballistic and emission theories, and detailed proposals about how light interacts with gravity and with matter. What unites them is a refusal of the standard answer that light is "both a wave and a particle" and that the question stops there. The researchers documented here treat that formula as a contradiction given a name rather than an explanation, and the persistence of the contradiction for over a century as evidence that the underlying model is wrong, not that nature is inscrutable.

title: Natural Philosophy Wiki
content_preview:
The Lorentz force is the force exerted on a charged particle by electric and magnetic fields, F = q ( E + v × B ). Together with Maxwell's equations , which govern the fields themselves, it constitutes classical electromagnetic theory : the equations say what the fields do, and the Lorentz force says what the fields do to charges .
The standard account
The expression is older than its name. Hermann Grassmann published the equivalent force between current elements in 1845; Maxwell gave the form in the Treatise (1873); Oliver Heaviside wrote it for a moving point charge in 1889; and Hendrik Lorentz made it the foundation of his electron theory in the 1890s, which is how it acquired his name.
Its content is straightforward and heavily used. The electric term acts along E regardless of the particle's motion. The magnetic term acts perpendicular to both the velocity and B , does no work, and bends a charged particle moving in a uniform magnetic field into a circle of radius mv ⁄ qB — the basis of the cyclotron, the mass spectrometer, magnetic focusing in electron optics, and the operation of every electric motor.
Two features are important for what follows. First, the Lorentz force is not derivable from Maxwell's equations; it is an independent postulate of the theory, added alongside them. Second, the Grassmann–Lorentz form is not the only candidate. The original force law of André-Marie Ampère , published between 1820 and 1825, contains a component acting along the direction of current flow, which Grassmann's does not. For a complete closed circuit the two laws give identical results, so ordinary laboratory and engineering practice cannot distinguish them. They differ only for isolated current elements — that is, where a circuit is broken, deformed, or destroyed.
On this wiki
The Lorentz force is one of the most heavily contested items in the literature collected here, and the objections are of several distinct kinds. The broader picture is set out at Electromagnetism

Carezani's answer is that the question does not arise. Autodynamics discards the two frames in relative motion on which the notion of invariance is built, replaces the Lorentz equations with his own, and treats the phenomenon and the observer as forming a single physical system. Invariance as a semantic question
Carezani's substantive point is that "invariance" as usually stated conceals a change in what is being described. Maxwell's equations at rest, transformed to a system in relative motion, are the same as saying that the phenomenon they describe is in motion with respect to the observer. Working the classical equations into general form, he notes the standard result: an observer in motion who sees an electric field E will also see a magnetic field H . His question is whether that counts as invariance. "The equations are 'invariant,' but a different phenomenon appears when the observer, or the phenomenon, is in motion. The Autodynamics form

Low Level Measurements is a four-page article by Leslee A Kulba , published in 2010 in issue 48 of the Electric Spacecraft Journal , the journal's final double issue. It is the seventh part of the ten-part handbook on perpetual motion and its testing that Kulba, the journal's technical editor, contributed to that issue, and at four pages it is one of the two longest practical articles in the set.
The text of the article has not been recoverable, and this page describes its subject and its place in the series rather than its argument.
The subject
Low-level measurement is the art of measuring voltages, currents, charges and resistances small enough that the measurement apparatus is a significant part of the phenomenon. It has a substantial professional literature — the standard work is Keithley Instruments' Low Level Measurements Handbook , which shares this article's title and was in its sixth edition at the time — and it is relevant here because the anomalies claimed in this field are characteristically small differences between large numbers, which is the regime in which the errors below are decisive.
The noise floor
There is a floor below which no amount of care helps, and it is set by physics rather than by the instrument. Johnson–Nyquist noise, present in any resistance at any temperature above absolute zero, has a root-mean-square voltage of √(4 kTRB ) — about 1.3 microvolts across a one-megohm resistor in a 1 Hz bandwidth at room temperature, and growing as the square root of both resistance and bandwidth. Shot noise sets a corresponding limit on current measurement, and 1/ f or flicker noise dominates at low frequencies, which is exactly where slow drifting measurements live.

content_preview:
Mach's principle is the proposal that inertia is not a property a body possesses on its own, but an effect of that body's relation to all the other matter in the universe — so that local inertial frames are determined by the distant stars rather than by absolute space.
The standard account
The idea originates with the Austrian physicist and philosopher Ernst Mach (1838–1916), whose Die Mechanik in ihrer Entwicklung (1883) attacked Newton 's use of absolute space. Newton had argued from his rotating-bucket experiment that the curved surface of the water reveals rotation with respect to space itself. Mach replied that the experiment shows nothing of the kind: the water rotates with respect to the fixed stars, and nobody has performed — or could perform — the experiment with the rest of the universe removed. On Mach's reading, inertial resistance is a relational quantity, produced by the surrounding masses.
Einstein was strongly influenced by this argument and coined the term "Mach's principle" in 1918, hoping General Relativity would embody it. It does so only partially. General relativity does predict genuine relational effects — the Lense–Thirring frame dragging of 1918, measured by the LAGEOS satellites and by Gravity Probe B in 2011 — but it also admits solutions that are plainly non-Machian, notably Gödel's 1949 rotating universe and the empty Minkowski spacetime, in which inertial frames exist with no matter at all to define them. Brans and Dicke proposed their scalar–tensor theory in 1961 explicitly to make gravitation more Machian by tying the gravitational "constant" to the mass distribution; solar-system tests have since pushed its coupling parameter to values where it is observationally close to general relativity.
There is no agreed formulation of the principle. Physicists have catalogued a dozen or more inequivalent statements travelling under the same name, and whether general relativity satisfies any of them remains genuinely disputed inside mainstream

Magnetism is the set of phenomena by which certain materials and moving charges attract or repel one another without contact: the behaviour of lodestone and iron, of the compass needle, of the electric current and the coil.
It is among the oldest observed effects in physics and among the least explained. Mainstream physics describes magnetism with great precision and declines to say what it is ; a large part of the literature catalogued on this wiki holds that this is not a limitation to be tolerated but the central problem, and that magnetism has a mechanical cause which can be shown.
The mainstream account
In the standard treatment magnetism is one aspect of a single electromagnetic field , unified with electricity by Maxwell in the 1860s.
A magnetic field B is produced by moving electric charge — a current in a wire, or the intrinsic circulation attributed to electrons within matter — and acts only on charge that is itself moving, through the Lorentz force, which is perpendicular both to the velocity and to the field. Because that force is always perpendicular to the motion, a magnetic field does no work on a moving charge; it changes direction, not speed.
Permanent magnetism in iron is attributed to electron spin rather than to orbital motion. Spin is treated as an intrinsic quantum property carrying a magnetic moment, and in a ferromagnet the exchange interaction — a quantum effect with no classical counterpart — aligns these moments across domains, so that their contributions add instead of cancelling.
There are no magnetic monopoles: cutting a magnet in half yields two magnets, and Maxwell's equations record this as ∇· B = 0. In special relativity the distinction between the electric and magnetic fields becomes frame-dependent — what one observer describes as a magnetic force another describes as electric — which is taken to show that the two are aspects of one object rather than two phenomena.

Malcolm Davidson is a researcher in electromagnetic theory and digital electronic design, known chiefly as a long-time collaborator of the British electronics engineer Ivor Catt . Together with Catt and David S. Walton he formed the "Catt, Davidson and Walton" partnership whose late-1970s papers and books challenged the conventional textbook treatment of Maxwell's displacement current.
Biography
Little biographical information about Davidson has been published. He became associated with Ivor Catt and Dr. David S. Walton during the 1970s, when the three worked jointly on the theory and practice of high-speed digital logic and on the electromagnetic behaviour of capacitors and transmission lines. As part of this research Davidson interviewed H. J. Josephs, one of the recognised authorities on the work of Oliver Heaviside, whose concept of "energy current" underlies the group's approach to electromagnetism.
Scientific contributions
Davidson's principal contribution lies in the group's re-examination of the capacitor. Walton had proposed that a capacitor is properly understood as a transmission line; Davidson argued that on this view the exponential RC charging waveform must be built up from a series of small discrete steps, a result which supported the transmission-line model of the capacitor. This line of reasoning led, in May 1976, to the group's conclusion that the concept of displacement current is unnecessary — a step central to what Catt later called "Theory C".
The resulting arguments were set out in two articles in Wireless World : "Displacement current" (December 1978) and "The History of Displacement Current" (March 1979), both co-authored by Catt, Davidson and Walton. The articles provoked considerable controversy among electrical engineers and physicists.

Manfred Geilhaupt is a German physicist associated with the Hochschule Niederrhein, the University of Applied Sciences at Krefeld and Mönchengladbach. He works on the origin of the physical constants, and in particular on the proposition that the rest mass of the electron, its charge and the fine structure constant can be derived rather than measured, by combining general relativity with the principles of thermodynamics.
Approach
Geilhaupt describes his programme as a "GR+TD" one — general relativity supplemented by thermodynamics, and specifically by the second law. A recurring theme is the set of large dimensionless numbers relating atomic to cosmological scales, in the tradition of Eddington and of Dirac's large numbers hypothesis. His two conference contributions recorded here address the two halves of that theme: one the relations among the measured constants themselves, the other the numerical span between the electron and the universe.

Abstract
The Earth was created in six days? This paraphrase from Genesis in the Bible may be surpassed in absurdity by fanciful "creation" theories in older civilizations of the world, but this belief has endured for 2,000 years without any physical evidence or logical reason to support it.
Overview
Myers — a retired U.S. Navy cryptologist who describes himself as "a non-scientist (cryptolinguist/codebreaker) with no degrees" — argues that the "hoax" of his title is not the Genesis account itself but its secular descendant: Kant's Nebular Hypothesis of 1755 as modified by Laplace in 1796, which holds that the Earth condensed rapidly from a cloud of gas and dust about 4.5 billion years ago and has kept the same size ever since. In his reading, a creation myth was replaced by a scientific one that shares its essential defect, a planet made all at once and thereafter fixed.
Against this he sets a growth model he calls "Accreation" — creation by accretion — in which a captured comet fragment in solar orbit grows continuously by external accretion of meteoritic mass and dust, by internal thermal expansion of a gravitationally heated core, and by volcanism that builds an atmosphere and surface water. The Earth on this account is "still a young planet and destined to continue growing forever". The paper's polemical centre is the rejection of subduction , which Myers calls "not only false, but physically impossible" and "one of the most egregious and avoidable blunders in the history of science". Its practical demand is that NOAA and the National Geodetic Survey recalculate the Earth's diameter and publish a revised datum to replace NAD83, from which a rate of expansion into the future could be computed.

Martin Fleischmann , FRS (born March 29, 1927 in Karlovy Vary , Czechoslovakia ) is an electrochemist at the University of Southampton and a Fellow of the Royal Society . He is best known for his controversial work with his colleague Stanley Pons on cold fusion using palladium in the 1980s and '90s. He was also the first observer of what was later called Surface Enhanced Raman Scattering .
On March 23, 1989 while they were researchers at the University of Utah , he and Stanley Pons announced "N-Fusion" which was quickly labeled by the press as cold fusion -- a result previously thought to be unattainable. After a short period of public acclaim, the pair were attacked widely for sloppy, unreproducible research and inaccurate results, as Fleischmann predicted they would be. Fleischmann, Pons and the researchers who replicated the effect remain convinced the effect is real, but sceptics who oppose them are convinced it is not.
In 1992, Fleischmann moved to France with Pons, to work at the IMRA laboratory (part of Technova Corporation, a subsidiary of Toyota); the laboratory closed in 1998 after exhausting a research investment of $12 million USD. The pair parted ways in 1995, and Fleischmann returned to Southampton, where he remained as of 1999. title: Natural Philosophy Wiki
content_preview:
Mass is the property by which a body resists being accelerated and by which it gravitates. Those are two distinct descriptions — inertial mass, defined by Newton's second law, and gravitational mass, defined by the law of gravitation — and the fact that they agree is a measured result rather than a definition.
Newton took the equality for granted; Loránd Eötvös tested it around 1900 with a torsion balance, and modern experiments, including the MICROSCOPE satellite mission, have confirmed it to roughly one part in 10 15 . Einstein made the equality a postulate, the equivalence principle, and built general relativity on it. Special relativity added a second relation: the energy content of a body at rest is E = mc 2 . In modern usage the mass of a particle means its invariant rest mass; the older notion of a "relativistic mass" increasing with speed has largely been abandoned in the professional literature in favour of speaking about relativistic momentum and energy, though it survives in textbooks.
What mass actually is remains open even on the mainstream account. The Higgs mechanism, confirmed in its broad outline by the 2012 discovery of the Higgs boson, supplies masses to the elementary particles, but the values are free parameters fitted to experiment rather than predicted. And the Higgs accounts for only a small fraction of the mass of ordinary matter: the great majority of a proton's mass is the binding energy of the field inside it. Nothing in the Standard Model explains why inertia exists at all.

Three arguments about mass run through the literature collected here.

Mass Photon Theory was a live session presented by Henri Corniere on 18 March 2023 in the John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society live session series.
A single ponderable tiny photon frees the mind of old ways of thinking and opens up new paths to a broad field of investigation where the very large can then be described and explained by the very small.
Summary
Henri Corniere 's presentation of his massive photon hypothesis, given a fortnight after James Keene previewed the paper for the society. Ian J Cowan hosted and advanced the six slides on request, Corniere having been unable to share his own screen.
He introduced himself briefly. He took a master's degree in science at Nantes and was dissatisfied enough with what he was taught — relativity, and a photon with no mass — that he did not continue in the academy, working instead as a field electronics engineer; retirement gave him the time to return to it. His statement of method was that nature does not care about our theories, that theories must fit the data rather than the reverse, and that the past mistakes have to be corrected before anything else can proceed.

The hypothesis is that the photon has a small rest mass and that space is filled with a photon gas, which he treats with the nineteenth-century kinetic theory of gases — asking explicitly whether that theory still works when the particle size drops by a factor of about a million.

Abstract
In (Assis 1998, pp. 241-249) and (Assis 1999, pp. 199-205) it was said that if we double the average matter density of the distant universe (galaxies), while keeping constant the matter density of the earth and all sizes and distances, the acceleration of free fall halves (that is, goes to 4.9m/s 2 instead of the usual 9.8m/s 2 ). Guala-Valverde concluded that in this case the acceleration of free fall should go to (9.8m/s 2 ) / 2, see (Guala-Valverde 1999a and 1999b, p. 25). But this was only due to a misunderstanding. Guala-Valverde was thinking on doubling the average inertial mass density of distant galaxies, while Assis was talking of doubling the average gravitational mass density of distant matter (see (Assis 1998, pp. 207, 211 and 246) or (Assis 1999, pp. 170, 174 or 204). This solves all misunderstandings. That is, Guala-Valverde and Assis agree that doubling the gravitational mass density of distant matter (while keeping unalterable Hubble's constant, the gravitational mass of the earth and its radius) will make the acceleration of free fall go to 4.9 m/s 2 . So our results are not clashing, it was all due to a misunderstanding.

In one of the earliest, and arguably the most eloquent, of the great texts advocating the systematic application of the empirical method, we find these wise words: ?Nor shall we be led to the doctrine of atoms, which implies the hypothesis of a vacuum and that of the unchangeableness of matter (both false assumptions) ...." It is only fitting that at the very outset of the scientific venture the wisest of mankind should have put his finger on what was to prove the most stubborn obstacle (I call it The Fatal Trap) to obtaining a rationally coherent, empirically grounded conception of the world. The first is that it is wholly unable to account for change: the atoms, by definition, are unchanging, and change is totally inapplicable to a vacuum ? itself, as spatially extended nothing, an absurdity, as many of the Greeks, Aristotle among them, saw. The second is that there can exist no causal ground for attractions and repulsions between the atoms across empty space. And the attempt to resolve this by postulating a plenum merely creates further insoluble problems. Maurice Félix Charles Allais (31 May 1911 – 9 October 2010) was a French economist and physicist. He was the 1988 winner of the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics "for his pioneering contributions to the theory of markets and efficient utilization of resources." Although he is best known for his work in economics, Allais also carried out extensive experimental and theoretical work in physics, and is remembered for the Allais Effect , an anomalous behaviour of a pendulum reported during solar eclipses.

Biography
Maurice Allais was born on 31 May 1911 in Paris, France, into a modest family; his father was a shopkeeper and his grandfather a carpenter. His father, taken prisoner during the First World War, died in Germany in 1915, an event that affected Allais deeply. Despite his young age, he resolved to honour his father's name.
Allais studied at the Lycée Lakanal and then entered the École Polytechnique in Paris, from which he graduated at the top of his class. He continued his studies at the École Nationale Supérieure des Mines de Paris, and later obtained a doctorate in engineering from the University of Paris (Faculty of Science) in 1949. From 1944 he served as Professor of Economics at the École Nationale Supérieure des Mines de Paris, and in 1946 he became director of its Economic Analysis Centre. He also held teaching positions at other institutions, including the University of Paris X–Nanterre.
Allais died on 9 October 2010 in Saint-Cloud, near Paris, at the age of 99.

Abstract
Based on the work of Jacobson [1] and Gibbons, [2] Schiller [3] has shown not only that a maximum force follows from general relativity, but that general relativity can be derived from the principle of maximum force. In the present paper an alternative derivation of maximum force is given. Inspired by the equivalence principle, the approach is based on a modification of the well known special relativity equation for the velocity acquired from uniform proper acceleration. Though in Schiller's derivation the existence of gravitational horizons plays a key role, in the present derivation this is not the case. In fact, though the kinematic equation that we start with does exhibit a horizon, it is not carried over to its gravitational counterpart. A few of the geometrical consequences and physical implications of this result are discussed.
Overview
Christoph Schiller had shown that a maximum force F MAX = c 4 /4 G follows from general relativity, and that general relativity can be recovered from it — the maximum force playing "the same role for general relativity as the maximum speed plays for special relativity." Abstract
Displacement current was originally conceived by James Clerk Maxwell in 1861 in connection with linear polarization in a dielectric solid which he believed to pervade all of space. Modern textbooks however adopt a different approach. The official teaching today is that displacement current is a consequence of extending the original solenoidal Ampère’s Circuital Law to embrace the conservation of electric charge. Maxwell's equations are the four coupled partial differential equations that, together with the Lorentz force law , constitute classical electromagnetic theory : Gauss's law for the electric field, the absence of magnetic monopoles, Faraday's law of induction, and the Ampère–Maxwell law with its displacement-current term.
The standard account
James Clerk Maxwell built the theory in stages — "On Physical Lines of Force" (1861–62), which developed it from a mechanical model of molecular vortices in an aether ; "A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field" (1865); and the Treatise on Electricity and Magnetism (1873). The decisive step was the displacement current , a term added to Ampère's circuital law which makes the system consistent with conservation of charge and, crucially, yields a wave equation. The waves travel at 1⁄√(ε₀μ₀), a quantity computable from purely electrostatic and magnetostatic measurements, and Maxwell found it equal within experimental error to the measured speed of light — the identification of light as an electromagnetic wave.
Two historical facts matter for what follows. First, the four equations universally taught today are not the ones Maxwell wrote. The Treatise presented a larger system — commonly counted as twenty equations in twenty variables, using quaternion notation — and it was Oliver Heaviside who in the mid-1880s recast them into the compact four-equation vector form, discarding the scalar and vector potentials as primary quantities. Second, the equations govern the fields only; they do not by themselves say what force a field exerts on a charge. That requires the separately postulated Lorentz force.
The equations are Lorentz-invariant as they stand, which is why they required no amendment when special relativity appeared in 1905; historically the influence ran the other way, with electromagnetism serving as the model relativity was built to match. Title Maxwell's Equations Do Not Fit Special Relativity Theory
Read in full Link to paper
Author(s) Janusz Dyonizy Laski
Keywords maxwell , special relativity
Published 2009
No. of pages 7
Abstract
There are two versions of Maxwell's equations. The classical version uses the Coulomb gauge and the relativistic version has electrodynamic potentials fulfilling the non-homogeneous equations for waves. With the use of the Lorenz gauge such equations have been obtained from the fourth Maxwell's equation and the equation for potentials of vector of electric intensity E . We show that the last equation after differentiation in time and multiplication by dielectric permittivity is similar to the fourth Maxwell's equation. We also show that after obvious corrections the equations are equivalent. We claim that in the fourth Maxwell's equation, instead of the vector of electric current density j , its irrotational component should only be applied. We also claim that in the equation for potentials of vector E instead of vector A there should be only its solenoidal component. It is shown that the corrected form of these two equations is fully consistent with the rest of Maxwell's equations. As the result of replacing vectors j and A by their proper components the problem of different gauges disappeared. Only one gauge i.e. that of Lorenz with a changed sign is shown to be necessary. As the result of the proposed modification in the case of waves, the wave equations for the potentials - as well as for the field vectors - are homogeneous. It is not so in the relativistic version of Maxwell's equations. We claim that the classical Maxwell's equations in the proposed version are fully consistent, satisfactory and do not fit the Special Relativity Theory.

Mechanical Perpetual Motion is a four-page article by Leslee A Kulba , published in 2010 in issue 48 of the Electric Spacecraft Journal , the journal's final double issue. It opens the ten-part handbook on perpetual motion and its testing that Kulba, the journal's technical editor, contributed to that issue, and it takes the oldest and simplest form of the claim: a machine of weights, wheels and levers that is supposed to run on its own arrangement.
The text of the article has not been recoverable, and this page describes its subject and its place in the series rather than its argument.
The subject
The overbalanced wheel
The archetype is a wheel whose weights swing further from the axis on the descending side than on the ascending one, so that the descending side is always heavier and the wheel is always turning. It is the oldest mechanical proposal of its kind: Bhāskara II described a version with mercury-filled spokes in India around 1150, and the sketchbook of Villard de Honnecourt, from about 1230, contains a wheel hung with mallets on the same principle. Robert Fludd's water-screw mill of 1618 — a mill that pumps back its own water — is the hydraulic cousin.
The generic answer to all of them is a counting argument rather than an appeal to authority. Moving the weights out on the descending side does increase each weight's torque, but the same geometry that moves them out puts fewer of them on that side, and the two effects cancel exactly. Simon Stevin had shown the same kind of thing in 1586 with the chain draped over a pair of inclined planes: if it did not balance it would move forever, which he took as absurd, and the figure was carved on his tombstone.

Overview
The book develops relational mechanics , a quantitative implementation of the ideas of Leibniz, Berkeley, and Mach in which all dynamics is expressed purely through relational quantities — the distances, relative radial velocities, and relative radial accelerations between material bodies — with no reference to absolute space or time. Assis replaces Newton's gravitational force with a velocity- and acceleration-dependent Weber-type force , and shows how this implements Mach's principle, deriving inertia from the gravitational interaction of a body with the distant matter of the universe. Abstract
In this paper, I refocus on the first one of the findings that I described in: Did Einstein cheat? The unexplained advance of Mercury's perihelion can be found without any artifice, by using the motion of the solar system inside the Milky Way, just by applying the Maxwell Analogy (which has firstly been suggested by Heavyside) and by using the proper velocities' definitions.
Overview
Mercury's Perihelion Advance is Caused by Our Milky Way is a four-page paper by Thierry De Mees (dated December 2004, updated July 2007), published in the General Science Journal . It restates the first result of his earlier Did Einstein Cheat?
The framework is the Maxwell Analogy for gravitation — Heaviside's 1893 proposal that gravity, like electromagnetism, has a second field generated by moving mass. De Mees writes the four analogue equations, calls the second field gyrotation Ω, and adds one departure from Heaviside and Jefimenko: the velocity entering the induction must be a "local absolute speed" defined relative to "the local stationary gravitation field", not relative to an observer. "Only gravitation fields can be regarded as 'local immobile' references."
Applied to Mercury, the argument runs:
The Sun's own spin is too slow to matter, but the Sun moves through the Milky Way at v 1 ≈ 235 km/s.

Mercury's own orbital speed is v 2 = 47.9 km/s, so v 1 ² = 24 v 2 ², turning the extra term into 12 G mM v 2 ²cos²α / r²c².

Metaphysics of Relativity Does Not Make Sense was a live session presented by Roger J Anderton on 31 May 2025 in the John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society live session series.
Among the many things missed out from being taught to physics students is metaphysics. So, they are not told that from the perspective of Newtonian physics that the metaphysics of Einstein's relativity does not make sense. Hosted by Roger Anderton.
Summary
Roger J Anderton 's subject is a gap in the physics curriculum. Metaphysics — the assumptions about time, space, causation and existence that a theory must presuppose before its equations can be interpreted — is not taught to physics students, and his contention is that the omission is what makes the disagreement about relativity irresolvable.
The metaphysics of Newton
He set out the framework a student absorbs implicitly from Newtonian mechanics. Absolute space, existing independently of the objects in it and remaining even if all matter vanished. Absolute time, flowing uniformly and, in Newton's own words, without relation to anything external. Determinism: given all positions and velocities, past and future are fixed, and the universe is a clockwork — which raises, though he did not press it, the question of who made the clock. Space and time as substances rather than relations, a view Leibniz disputed. Objects with well-defined identities and trajectories against that fixed background. And forces as real physical causes, gravity acting at a distance in a way Newton himself found puzzling and declined to frame a hypothesis about.
Anderton entered one correction on his own behalf: Newton did discuss relative space and relative time, and the assistant's presentation of him as concerned only with the absolute is not quite fair.

Michael Faraday (22 September 1791 – 25 August 1867) was an English experimentalist whose discoveries founded the practical science of electricity and whose idea of lines of force filling the space around magnets and charges became, after Maxwell gave it mathematical form, the field concept of modern physics.
Faraday came to science without a university education. Apprenticed to a bookbinder, he was taken on at the Royal Institution as Humphry Davy's laboratory assistant in 1813 and remained there for the rest of his working life. In 1821 he produced the first continuous electromagnetic rotation — a wire circling a magnetic pole — the ancestor of every electric motor. On 29 August 1831 he demonstrated electromagnetic induction: a changing current in one coil wound on an iron ring induced a transient current in a second coil, with no contact between them. Within months he had built the homopolar or "Faraday disc" generator, in which a copper disc spun between the poles of a magnet delivers a steady current. In 1833–34 he established the laws of electrolysis, showing that the mass deposited at an electrode is proportional to the quantity of charge passed — the first strong quantitative evidence for a natural unit of electricity. In 1845 he found that a magnetic field along the path of light rotates its plane of polarisation (the Faraday effect), the first demonstrated link between light and magnetism, and in the same year identified diamagnetism. His experimental notebooks were published as Experimental Researches in Electricity (1839–1855), written almost entirely without equations.

Michael Meade Steinbacher was an American photographer, based at Whitewater in the California desert, who applied a camera and a great deal of fieldwork to geology. He contributed two papers to the Natural Philosophy Alliance and led its geology field tours , taking participants through the mountains and deserts of the American west to look at landforms in the light of his own reading of them.
His thesis, set out in " A New Approach to Mountain Formation " (2011), is that mountain ranges are lithified dunes. He proposes that a transient high-energy plasma discharge once enveloped the Earth, filling the air with dust and sand driven by extreme winds; that higher ground acted as a snow fence, so that material drifted behind it in self-perpetuating deposits; and that electromagnetic effects — he names the Bennett pinch — gathered and hardened the airborne material. Rain and floodwater then cut the dunes into a slurry which slumped into stratified alluvial fans, and further electrical discharge converted the fresh deposits into granite, sandstone, schist and basalt. The "rivers of fire" of ancient legend he reads as discharges cutting drainage channels by something like industrial electrical discharge machining. A companion paper, " The Consequences of a Reversal of the Rotation of Earth " (2012), pursues a related line.
The approach draws on two sources. One is the worldwide similarity of catastrophe traditions, which Steinbacher — following Velikovsky — takes to record an event within human memory; he opens the 2011 paper by noting that he is not religious and that a single such story would not have interested him. The other is Electric Universe plasma cosmology, and in particular Anthony Peratt's comparison of petroglyph forms with instabilities observed in high-energy laboratory discharges.

Michael Holdt Twichell is an American electrical and software engineer and a self-published theorist, known in the New Energy and Tesla-research community for Aether Gravity — a proposal that gravity is not a property of space curvature but the observable consequence of matter absorbing the aether around it . He has set the theory out in two self-published volumes, The Twichell Manuscript — Volume I: Aether Gravity (2011) and Physics of the Dark Matter: The Proton Magnet (2017), and has presented it four times at the TeslaTech ExtraOrdinary Technology Conference.
His position is a full-space one: he holds that the replacement of the nineteenth-century aether by the empty-space model of relativity was a wrong turn, and that restoring a material medium removes the need for much of what he regards as the over-complication of modern physics.
Aether Gravity
The central claim of the first volume is a mechanism rather than a field equation. Matter, on Twichell's account, continuously absorbs the aether in which it sits; the resulting inflow towards a mass is what is observed as gravitational attraction. Weight is therefore a consequence of a flow, not of a geometric property of spacetime.
From that single mechanism he argues for explanations of a range of otherwise unconnected phenomena, among them plate tectonics and the inner–outer core structure of the Earth, supernovae and black holes, the Pioneer anomaly , the Allais effect and the Coriolis effect . He also treats the theory as the route to gravity control, and has argued that the same principle was known to ancient civilizations — a theme he developed in a 2015 interview with Open Minds TV and in his later conference talks.

title: Michelson interferometer
content_preview:
The Michelson interferometer is an optical instrument that splits a single beam of light into two paths, sends them along separate arms to mirrors, recombines them, and reads the resulting interference fringes. Because the fringe pattern responds to differences in the optical path travelled by the two beams, the instrument converts a change far smaller than a wavelength of light into a visible shift — which is what has made it, for more than a century, the most sensitive general-purpose measuring device in physics.
How it works
A half-silvered beam splitter divides the incoming light. One part travels to a mirror at the end of arm 1 and returns; the other travels to a mirror at the end of arm 2 and returns. The two returning beams recombine at the splitter and are observed together. If the two round trips take exactly the same time the beams arrive in phase; any difference produces a proportional displacement of the fringes. Rotating the whole apparatus, changing an arm length, changing the medium in an arm, or changing the speed of the instrument through whatever the light propagates in will all, on one theory or another, alter the fringe position.
Albert A. Michelson built the first version in 1881 in Potsdam and, with Edward Morley , a far more sensitive one mounted on a stone slab floating in mercury for the 1887 Michelson–Morley experiment at the Case School of Applied Science in Cleveland. That instrument had an effective arm length of about 11 metres, achieved by multiple reflections, and was expected to show a fringe shift of roughly 0.4 of a fringe as it was turned.
The design has outlived the question it was built to answer. Fourier-transform infrared spectrometers are Michelson interferometers with one moving mirror. Michelson himself used the principle to measure stellar diameters — the first was Betelgeuse in 1920 — and to define the metre in terms of the wavelength of cadmium light. Abstract
Despite the null interpretation of their experiment by Michelson and Morley, it is quantitatively shown that the outcomes of the original experiment, and all subsequent repetitions, never were null. Additionally, due to an incorrect inter-session averaging, the non-null results are even larger than reported. Contrary to the received view, Illingworth's and other repetitions of the experiment were consistent with Miller's positive results. On the theoretical side, a new systematic error is uncovered: the angle between the projection of earth's velocity on the plane of the interferometer and the reference arm of the apparatus has been practically ignored. This phase angle produces a noticeable change in the position of the peaks from one turn to the next of the interferometer. Hence, the data analysis cannot be based on the average of fringe shifts during a session, but rather on the calculation of individual speed for each turn. This procedure was applied to the only two sessions reported in detail in the literature: Miller's September 23, 1925 at 03:02 in Mount Wilson and Illingworth's July 9, 1927 at 11:00 in Pasadena. Surprisingly, it was found that in both cases the measured speeds exactly correspond to the projection of earth's orbital velocity only. As a result, the evidence against a preferred frame completely disappears.

Múnera, writing from the Centro Internacional de Física in Bogotá, returns to the primary literature of the Michelson-Morley Experiment and its repetitions between 1887 and 1930 and asks a narrow, checkable question: what did the experimenters actually measure, as distinct from what they conclude

Abstract
The Michelson-Morley Interferometer Experiment of 1887 is often cited as one of the cornerstones (and perhaps THE cornerstone) upon which Einstein built his theory of special relativity. Allegedly, it “proved” there was no aether. Once Einstein postulated that the speed of light was invariant, the only explanation that became accepted was that time slowed and length contracted due to relative motion according to the Lorentz Transformation formulae, adopted by Einstein as tenets of his special relativity. Despite subsequent experiments contradicting the alleged “null result,” reanalysis of the results indicating positive (“non-null”) results, and even maintaining the validity of the null result but explaining it via classical physics, the M&M Interferometer Experiment remains a special relativity foundation. However, if the limitation of the invariance of the speed of light is removed, the “null result” can be easily explained without resort to special relativity and its postulates of time dilation and length contraction. Year 1887
Michelson and Morley's interferometer, mounted on a stone slab floating in a trough of mercury.
The Michelson–Morley experiment of 1887 is the most consequential experiment in modern physics, and on this wiki the most closely examined. Performed by Albert A. Michelson and Edward W. Morley at the Case School in Cleveland, it used an interferometer to look for the change in the speed of light that should accompany the Earth's motion through a stationary aether .
It is universally taught as the null result that abolished the aether and cleared the way for special relativity . The critical literature catalogued here — more than sixty papers by some forty researchers — disputes that account on a single central point: the result was never null . What Michelson and Morley measured was a fringe shift smaller than predicted, but not zero; and when the experiment was continued for decades by Morley's collaborator Dayton C Miller , it yielded a small, systematic, repeatable signal that has never been satisfactorily explained away.
The experiment
An interferometer splits a beam of light along two perpendicular arms and recombines it. If the apparatus is moving through a light-carrying medium, the two round trips should take slightly different times, and rotating the apparatus should shift the interference fringes. From the Earth's orbital speed of about 30 km/s, Michelson and Morley expected a shift of roughly four-tenths of a fringe.
