Summary
An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with Ian Cohen, James Keene , Bob Gray , Carl and Alex, the whole of it on dark matter. Hu's microphone was barely audible for the first half — a Windows update had reset the level — so Ian carried much of the discussion, and Hu twice handed the chair over while attending to his mother.
Ian: are spiral galaxies spiral?
Ian's proposal, which he has raised before and thinks neglected, is that what we see in the night sky is not a contemporaneous snapshot. An object is visible only if it happened to be at a distance of X light years at the moment X years ago when it emitted the light; if it was elsewhere then, the light has already passed us or has not yet arrived. Looking at a nebula whose near side is a million light years away and whose far side is two million, we are combining events separated by a million years.
From that he draws two conclusions. First, that the gravitational effects attributed to dark matter may simply be matter we cannot see — ordinary matter, of the kind found in a laboratory, that is not at the right distance for its light to reach us now. He prefers to call this dark stuff , declining the mainstream term. Second, and more provocatively, that spiral galaxies may not be spiral. His tentative position is that they are elliptical or spherical bodies whose apparent shape is the composite of parts seen at different epochs as the object rotates.

An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with Bill Lucas , James Keene , Bob Gray and a new participant, Toby. The theme was set by Lucas — how to judge between competing theories — and it turned into a sustained cross-examination of his own.
Distinti, and the case for polytheism
Lucas had found a YouTube channel by Robert Distinti, an electrical engineer with a couple of hundred videos, and recommended it as a third party critical of everyone's theories rather than of any one of them. Hu played David de Hilster 's review of Distinti's latest.
The point that stuck was Distinti's rule that a theory's ability does not prove its exclusivity: that a model gives good answers does not show no other model would give the same ones. De Hilster's illustration from his own experience was a dean telling him his thesis was ridiculous because Maxwell's equations are irrefutable — which, he said, misses that there may be another way to arrive at the same place. Distinti's remedy for what he calls polytheism — several theories fitting the same data — is to increase the sampling footprint until the candidates can be told apart, his example being two sine waves of different frequency that both pass through every measured point until one measures more finely.
Lucas drew from it the moral he cared about: a theory is never finished. General relativity was put forward to explain gravity, and when the Pioneer trajectories and the spiral arms did not fit, the response was to add dark matter and dark energy rather than to falsify anything.

Summary
An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with Ian Cohen, Bob Gray , Dennis Allen , Harry Ricker and Jim, given over entirely to unipolar induction — the Faraday disc. An email storm had been running all week on the subject, with messages arriving several times an hour, and this session was the attempt to settle it against the experimental record.
The question
When a cylindrical magnet is rotated about its own magnetic axis, does its field rotate with it?
Hu says no: put a compass beside the magnet, spin the magnet about its axis, and the compass will not move; nothing about the space around it changes. Field lines, on his account, are a mathematical device with no physical realization, so there is nothing there to be traced from one angular position to another. He predicted that iron filings on a paper over a spinning magnet would sit perfectly still.

Summary
Bob Gray presented an update on his classical electrodynamics research, hosted by Franklin Hu , with Bill Lucas , Ian Cohen, James Keene and Alistair Riddoch taking part.
Gray: from Weber to a generalized Maxwell system
Gray is looking for the simplest and most complete route to classical electrodynamics. His starting point is Weber electrodynamics, which is conventionally presented without fields at all: everything follows from a single potential energy function. He has taken that function and defined fields and potentials from it, arriving at four equations that look much like Maxwell's but carry three extra terms. Those terms come from the time derivative of the charge density, which appears in Weber's approach and, for reasons he cannot see, not in Maxwell's; set them to zero and the two systems coincide. He treats this as evidence that Maxwell's system comes up short.
What he wants and cannot yet get is the expression for the electrodynamic field that he was taught comes from special relativity. He would rather not import relativity into Weber to obtain it, and he reported a correction to his own understanding: Heaviside derived that same expression from Maxwell's equations in 1888, seventeen years before the relativity paper, so it does not depend on relativity at all. Lucas's The Universal Force derives it too, from six empirical laws of electrodynamics — more assumptions than Weber's one potential function, which is why Gray keeps looking.

Ian had gone to a lecture by Professor Peter Coles of Maynooth, given to Astronomy Ireland, on the centenary of the Eddington–Dyson eclipse measurement. He asked from the floor why no terrestrial experiment had been contemplated, and then put his own position: that general relativity as such — the space-time account — has not been verified, only certain peripheral anomalies. Coles replied that if one neglects all the evidence then of course there is no evidence, and the audience applauded. Ian's own description of the moment was fair to both sides: the speaker had said all the right things about science being open to question, was not hostile, and was courteous afterwards in the pub, but was plainly reluctant to engage, and the applause was for putting down a crank at the back.
He pressed two further points privately. On the standard rejoinder that GPS confirms general relativity daily, he answered that what GPS shows is the variation of atomic clock rates with gravitational potential, which is not general relativity as such; and he said that GPS contradicts special relativity, since the speed of light there is not independent of the observer's motion. An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with Alistair Riddoch , Ian Cohen, James Keene , Bill Lucas , Harry Ricker and Toby. It began with Riddoch's model of the vacuum and turned into an argument about what would count as doing science at all.
Infinity, and immutability
Riddoch opened with two things he had been turning over. The first was density: he had learned that relativity has the centre of a black hole infinitely dense, and wanted to know whether infinite density is even a possible thing. Hu's answer was that an infinity in a result is a red flag that something has gone wrong, and he made the same complaint about renormalization, which he calls dividing one infinity by another and keeping the answer. Ian agreed — thou shalt not divide by zero — and extended it to the big bang's infinitely small interval and infinitely great density, and to the Copenhagen picture, which appears to require an infinite speed of transmission where relativity has a finite one.
The second was the word immutable . Riddoch's own model has Planck-scale building blocks that have always existed and never change: not permeable, not compressible, not flexible. What changes is only their relative orientation, spin polarity and rate of rotation. Because they are not perfect spheres — their surfaces are wave-deformed — the gaps between them do change, alternating between hyperbolic tetrahedra and hyperbolic octahedra as the blocks turn. Those gaps are genuine void, with no properties at all except a shape, and the shape is defined entirely from outside: as he put it, it is the doughnut that defines the hole, not the hole.

Eugene presented what he calls the biogenic earthquake hypothesis, posted as a preprint on EarthArXiv: that microbial life beneath the surface may trigger earthquakes.
His argument runs in stages. The accepted limit on the depth of the biosphere — twelve to fifteen kilometres — rests on temperature and pressure limits he thinks badly underestimated: the most extreme organism known before 2018 tolerated 122 to 130 °C, and a strain found that year survives well beyond it. Set against models of the earth's interior composition, he arrives at a possible limit near seventy-five kilometres, which is deep enough to matter for earthquakes.
For how such organisms would feed, he pointed to a documented case: bacterial chains beneath the ocean floor that perform a distributed respiration, the deeper cells taking electrons from sulphur and passing them up the chain to cells at the surface that attach them to oxygen — effectively feeding on an electric current. Summary
Bob Gray presented on the internal consistency of Maxwell's equations, hosted by Franklin Hu , with Bill Lucas , Harry Ricker , James Keene , Cornelis Verhey , Carl and, later, David de Hilster .
Gray's claim
Gray had been working from Frederick David Tombe 's account of Maxwell's original equations, drawn from the 1861 and 1864 papers — twenty equations, presented in vector notation as eight. His question is not whether the equations agree with experiment but whether they are mathematically consistent among themselves: can one show, for a given equation, that the left-hand side genuinely equals the right?
To ask that he had to add assumptions, which he listed and offered for challenge: vacuum permittivity and permeability, one constitutive relation Tombe omits, point charges as an adequate approximation to their positions, the charge density as a sum of delta functions, the current density as charge density times a velocity, and expressions for the scalar and vector potentials for discrete charges. Everything then stands in fundamental quantities and the check can be made.
His result: it fails. Working out the divergence of E with those substitutions yields, on the right, a term containing the accelerations of the charges — the vector potential involves the current density, hence velocity, hence a time derivative giving acceleration — and there is nothing corresponding on the left. So the two sides cannot be equal in general.

The neutron lifetime measured from orbit
The paper reported the first space-based measurement: the MESSENGER spacecraft carries a neutron detector, and neutrons knocked out of Venus and Mercury by cosmic rays and counted at altitude give an estimate of how long they survive.
Hu set out why the item matters. The two laboratory methods — the bottle and the beam — do not agree: the beam gives about nine seconds longer than the bottle, against a lifetime near fourteen and a half minutes. If both are equally valid and give different answers, what is being measured? He returned to this as his standing test case, alongside the gravitational constant. He also noted how remarkable the number itself is: fourteen minutes is an age for a subatomic particle, closer to the decay of an atomic nucleus than to a muon. And he explained why the measurement is hard at all: a free neutron is nearly undetectable, and a detector is essentially a counter tube wrapped in a large block of wax, registering what the neutrons produce rather than the neutrons.
The verdict on the new result was that its uncertainty — something like ten to seventeen minutes — is far too wide to choose between the two laboratory values, though the group hopes to build a more precise instrument.

An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with James Keene , Ian Cohen, Alistair Riddoch , Carl and Bob Gray . It began with the clocks — Ian had arrived an hour early, the American and European changeovers being a fortnight apart — and with his account of daylight saving as a German wartime measure of 1916 to save coal, copied by Britain a month later. From the clocks it went to time itself and stayed there.
Is time quantized?
Keene holds that space, time and energy are all quantized, and that this is what makes his binary mechanics work: with those three quantities discrete, the quantities usually presented to students as fundamental physical constants become derivable rather than merely measured. He put the criterion plainly — by their fruits ye shall know them — and treated the quantization as a postulate justified by its utility, declining to go behind it. Asked why the world should be quantized, he said that is where science shades into philosophy and religion, and that he would leave it to others; he noted that Bill Lucas , asked the same, answers that God made it so, and that this is not where he himself will go.
Hu wanted a physical cause rather than a postulate, and offered one: that we are inside a computer. Nothing in a computer happens faster than the clock; each tick fixes a state; a bit is here or there and never half-way. Keene was sympathetic but said this is only another way of saying that space, time and energy are quantized.

An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu , with Dennis Allen , Harry Ricker , Ian Cohen and others, running on two threads: what a photon is, and how the earliest radio detector worked.
The shape of the photon
Hu repeated the claim he had made the previous week — that a photon occupies the space of a rod, still a compression wave, with the rod's orientation carrying the polarisation — and drew from it the distinction he thinks matters. At the high-frequency end everything looks like particles; at the radio end everything looks like waves; and that, he argued, is not a continuum of behaviour but two different things. Light generated by atomic electron transitions comes in these rod-like packets of fixed energy; a radio wave is more like an ocean wave, broad and of any amplitude.
Harry Ricker pressed the obvious objection: the electromagnetic spectrum appears continuous, from the very low frequencies once used to reach submerged submarines up to the extreme high frequencies — so where does one behaviour stop and the other begin? Hu's answer was that the boundary is technological, set by how fast electrons can be made to oscillate in a circuit, and he asked repeatedly what the highest radio frequency actually achievable is and where it sits on the spectrum. Ricker's own answer was that the spectrum is one thing described by two different models at the two ends, that the choice is a matter of which model one is using, and that this does not answer what either a photon or a radio wave physically is.

What is wrong with QED
Bob's summary of the paper's complaint was mathematical. Any QED calculation runs into infinities, and what is done with them depends on how the sums are taken and what is subtracted from what. The paper's first equation is the assignment of −1/12 to the sum of all the positive integers — traceable, through its references, to Euler — and this is used in the course of a calculation held up as physics' most accurate. Hu made the same complaint about renormalization: dividing infinity by infinity and keeping the answer.
The session then worked through the encyclopaedia articles on quantum electrodynamics, the quantum vacuum and the anomalous magnetic moment, reading them aloud. Hu could make nothing of the Feynman diagram — an electron and positron annihilating to a gamma ray which then produces a quark, an antiquark and a gluon, three things he takes not to exist — and said it looked like a cartoon.
Keene's objection went to the physics rather than the arithmetic. Most of what is going on, he said, is hidden in the diagram's vertices: when he derives Planck's constant from first principles it comes out as an elemental action divided by the fine structure constant, which implies well over a hundred events inside what is treated as a single Planck-constant event.

Summary
A general science chat hosted by Franklin Hu , standing in with no speaker scheduled, and used to make the first public presentation of an idea he had arrived at two or three months earlier. He stated it without preamble: the shape of a photon is a rod.
Why a shape at all
Hu's argument for insisting on one is that he is a physicalist — if it cannot be shown on a billiard table he does not believe it — and that the history of the DNA molecule is the model. The components were known long before anyone found the arrangement that fitted the data, and the helix ended the mystery. He wants the same for light rather than talk of a photon whose shape nobody will state.
A rod that is a wave
His second claim is that light is strictly a wave: he does not accept wave–particle duality, and says so rather than working around it. What he means by a rod is the wavelet one would get by dipping a rectangular object into a very narrow wave tank — a single pulse with a fixed width and height travelling in a straight line, not the great circular waves one normally makes.
He listed the properties this has to account for: light travels in rays, it does not disperse, and it is localised. His example was pair annihilation, where two back-to-back gamma rays strike specific spots in a silicon detector rather than smearing across it. A rod, he argued, has all three particle-like properties and remains a wave.
The inverse square law he handled by distinguishing the individual photon from the population: a photon from Alpha Centauri arrives at full amplitude, and it is only the number per unit area that thins with distance.
Polarisation, and no fields

Deriving the constants
Keene's claim for binary mechanics is that it derives what are called the fundamental constants — the speed of light, Planck's constant, the electron mass and others — from first principles, and that nobody else does. His first principles he described as minimal: the full quantisation of space, time and energy, quantisation being already accepted for charge.
The distinction he insisted on, and which Hu eventually accepted as a clean statement of where they differ, is between deriving a constant and showing interrelationships among constants. The literature is full of formulae relating the fine structure constant, the charge, the speed of light and the rest to one another, and Keene has no quarrel with that work — it is simply, as he put it, a different cage in the zoo. His rule is that unexplained data may not be explained by reference to other unexplained data. He noted, as support rather than opposition, that the standard model concedes it cannot derive any of these constants from its own principles.
Hu's counter, pressed several times, was that binary mechanics grounds out the same way one level down: it takes fundamental quantities of length, time and mass, and cannot say where those come from. Keene agreed without embarrassment — he has not attempted to, and there is an empty slot for anyone who wants to. Summary
An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with Dennis Allen , Bob, Roger, Bill Lucas , Alistair Riddoch and Ian Cohen, taking up an argument running on the society's email list.
Do a heavy and a light object really fall together?
Ian Cohen set out the case, carefully and at length, that they do not quite. The textbook derivation cancels the small mass from both sides and leaves the acceleration as GM/r ²; but the earth is not stationary, and the object attracts it too, so the relative acceleration is G(M+m)/r ². Two consequences follow. The heavier object accelerates very slightly faster. And, if the two experiments are run one after the other, the heavier object has slightly less distance to cover, because the earth has moved further to meet it. He was emphatic that this is not Aristotle vindicated — the difference is of the order of the object's mass to the earth's — but that it is not exactly zero either.
Hu accepted the distance argument readily and resisted the acceleration one, on the ground that inertial resistance rises in proportion to the force. Ian took him through it again, and the disagreement did not resolve.
Riddoch made the observation that clarified the case: if both objects are released at the same moment, the earth's movement toward them is common to both, so that effect drops out and only the acceleration difference remains — which is exactly the thought experiment Ian had proposed. He then scaled it up memorably: if the whole human population jumped a metre at once, the earth would move about a twelve-trillionth of a metre the other way, and when one person alone jumps, it moves eight billion times less.

Bob brought a paper he thought the group should see: a Liverpool group's experimental test of electron beam deflection in the fringing field of a solenoid, comparing three predictions — Weber's force equation, the Maxwell–Lorentz field treatment, and a commercial boundary-element package.
The result, which he showed from the plotted data, is that in the low velocity regime the Weber prediction tracks the measured deflections closely across three solenoid sizes while the Lorentz prediction is well off. Bob was careful to keep his own enthusiasm in check: he is a Weber partisan and said so, and added that Weber does not fit everything — at velocities near the speed of light it fails and the Lorentz treatment with the relativistic factor does better. His own standing question was why there is not one equation that works everywhere.
Hu found the more striking point to be that a law as basic as the Lorentz force is not confirmed here, and asked whether the paper had done the high-speed experiments itself. Bob was scrupulous: the paper cites others for that and he did not know how those were set up, so he would not speak for the authors.
The two then drew out the methodological difference. The disagreement
Gary's position, as Hu set it out from the video, is that light is strictly a particle: photons drawn as circles, with the polarisation an inherent property of each, no waves anywhere, and radio behaving the same way. Hu's is that a photon is a wavelet in a medium.
Hu was at pains to say how much he agrees. Treating photons as discrete clumps travelling through space with a definite volume and length is right; so is the account of what they do on arrival, jostling electrons; so is the photoelectric explanation, that what matters is the energy delivered per unit time rather than the total, with the fixed quantum hv per packet. His own picture of the photon as a rod maps onto Gary's circles, the rod's orientation supplying the polarisation.
His criticism is that the account is incomplete rather than wrong: it has to postulate a photon that stands in no relation to anything else known, and cannot say what it is made of. He used his standing image for this — the socks disappearing from the dryer, which little elves would explain perfectly consistently and without any way of being tested. Logical consistency, he said, is grossly insufficient. His own theory, he argued, sits one level below Gary's and says what the clump is.

Bob's answer: there is no magnetic field
Bob's case, developed over a long presentation, is that the magnetic field is not a physical field at all.
He began with terminology — field means several different things, and if one defines an electrodynamic field as force per unit charge on a test body, then B does not qualify, its units being wrong.
His alternative comes from Weber electrodynamics, where the force between two charged bodies is the Coulomb force multiplied by a coupling coefficient with a constant term, a velocity-dependent term and an acceleration-dependent term. His analogy was static against kinetic friction: nobody finds it strange that the coupling between two objects differs according to their relative motion. On this reading the magnetic field is simply that dynamic coupling, and the Coulomb field is the only real physical field.
He applied Occam's razor twice. First to William J Hooper , who identifies three electric fields — Coulomb, motional and transformer — which Bob tabulated to show that they differ precisely in how many time derivatives they carry: none, one, two. Second to the multipole expansion of the scalar potential, whose infinite series of terms would, on the same logic, give an infinite series of fields.

He remembers being struck at eighteen, in a first-year physics course, by the reciprocity paradox in special relativity — the question Dingle put, how a clock can be both faster and slower — and finding the answers unsatisfactory; but he went on with the mainstream.
What turned him was Al Kelly . He went, found colleagues in the audience dismissive, and was struck enough to look into it: the alternative readings of Michelson–Morley, an ether travelling with the earth in its orbit. There followed a correspondence in the Irish Times between Kelly and the academic community, including the Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies — founded in 1940 by de Valera on the model of Princeton's — whose replies Ian described as hostile and insulting.

Summary
John B Eichler — a computer scientist from the Illinois Institute of Technology who worked on Univac machines in the vacuum-tube era and designed blast shields for the Atomic Energy Commission — presenting the connection he sees between cosmology and expansion tectonics: that one must know how the solar system was assembled to understand what is happening to the earth.
Method
He began with what he thinks goes wrong. Where hands-on experiment is possible, results repeat; the earth and the universe do not allow it, and the strongest evidence is where laboratory work backs the theoretical construct. So one should question any proposed esoteric law that has no empirical verification, and remember that a concept being visualisable does not make it obey the laws of physics.
He then defined worldview as what the scientist brings to the table — the paradigms absorbed from classes and books. These are two-edged: without a framework we could not make sense of anything, and with one we cannot see past it. To a hammer, everything looks like a nail.

Abstract
A new cosmological theory is presented based on the proposition that all four metrical coefficients of space and time change with the cosmological expansion. Such a universal scale expansion would preserve the four-dimensional spacetime geometry and therefore by general relativity most physical relationships. In addition, if the scale expansion were exponential with time, all epochs would be equivalent. This is the first of a projected four-part series in Apeiron in which C Johan Masreliez sets out the Scale Expanding Cosmos (SEC) theory. The argument
Keene's paper takes its stand on a remark of Bell's own: that there is a way to escape the inference of superluminal speeds and spooky action at a distance, but that it involves absolute determinism. That escape is the freedom loophole , and Keene's claim is that binary mechanics occupies it — a local realist theory with exact time development laws, in which all action occurs over one length constant in one time constant, and in which the one-state quanta exist whether observed or not.
The consequence he draws is that entanglement experiments cannot settle the matter by themselves. Closing every other loophole leaves this one; to close it one would have to falsify the local realist theory directly — that is, falsify the quantisation of space, time and energy.
He was scathing about how the loophole is discussed, and this was the liveliest part of the paper: not merely deterministic but super -deterministic; not merely determinism but absolute determinism; not merely hard to imagine but impossible; not merely a question about free will but a loss of freedom to choose ; not merely a new question but unscientific. He called the vocabulary a propaganda ploy — believe in superluminal effects or be an anti-freedom jerk — and said the reason for it is precisely that the experiments alone cannot exclude the alternative.

Summary
An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with James Keene , Dennis Allen and others, given over to a set of experiments Keene had just been corresponding about — and to a long, patient and unresolved argument about whether his theory accounts for them.
Dmitriev's weight measurements
The experiments are Alexander Dmitriev's, at the technical university in St Petersburg, and Keene presented them as work that stands or falls on its own merits whatever anyone thinks of his interpretation.
They are all high-precision weighings of sealed containers in which something is stimulated. A brass rod heated ultrasonically loses weight over the period of heating. A piezoceramic pile heated by one degree shows the container's apparent mass fall while the temperature is held up, and stay down as long as it is held. Coils of optical fibre illuminated by helium and semiconductor lasers lose weight while the light is passing, and recover it a few seconds after the laser is switched off. And a container holding two rotors spinning in opposite directions — so that the total angular momentum is about zero — shows a mass difference that grows with the frequency of rotation.
On the last, Keene had written to Dmitriev because he could not tell from the paper which orientation weighed less, having predicted in the same email that it would be the horizontal rotor; the reply arrived a quarter of an hour before the session and confirmed it. Lucas gave his own reasons for rejecting the big bang while the sharing was sorted out. His derivation of gravity from electrodynamics has it arise from the force between vibrating neutral multipoles, which decay slowly — and that decay, on his account, produces the cosmic microwave background, so the observation usually taken as the strongest evidence for the big bang has another explanation. The same decay weakens the earth's field and causes it to expand, which he reads in the stretch marks on the ocean floor.
He then made a much larger claim, which should be read as his own: that of sixteen radiometric methods for dating the earth, only three gave an old age before radiohalos were understood, and that taking the halo patterns properly into account brings all sixteen into agreement at ten thousand years or less. He explained the mechanism he relies on — alpha particles from a decaying inclusion travelling a distance fixed by their energy and etching rings into the surrounding mineral, so that one can read off which isotopes were originally present rather than assuming all the lead came from uranium — and said the work was done at Oak Ridge and then ignored. Lucas — audible only with difficulty throughout — described work on coral and limestone. Coral lays down annual rings and, within them, ripples marking the days, so the oldest coral records years of some 486 days against the present 365. He reads this as the earth having expanded, on his own account through a decay in gravity, which he says he can predict; and he identifies two intervals in the record where the rate of change was different, which he associates with events in the biblical narrative.
He also reported that papers on the subject, some produced under NOAA contract, have been taken down from the internet, and that he has kept downloaded copies — drawing the parallel with what he sees in other fields the group works in.
Asked what causes the decay, he gave his own mechanism: within an atom each proton vibrates with respect to an electron, giving dipole, quadrupole or higher oscillations, and the net force between two atoms is proportional to the number of multipoles and the amplitude — most terms cancelling under spherical symmetry, which is why gravity is so many orders weaker. Summary
An open chat hosted by Franklin Hu with Bill Lucas , Ian Cohen, James Keene , Alistair Riddoch and Dennis Allen . Hu opened with a question rather than a topic: it is February 2020, a date that once sounded futuristic — why are there still such holes in physics, and why does nobody, orthodox or otherwise, know what gravity is?
Lucas on why
Lucas's answer was historical and political. He traced it to the American settlement between the established colonial churches and the revival movements, and argued that from about 1850 the separation of church and state was used to license a science defined by opposition to religion: what Maxwell and Ampère had called the Spirit of God became the electric field, and quantum mechanics took the universal wave function rather than the field as its object. He credited Poincaré with a meta-theory of theorems from logic applicable to all scientific theories, said Poincaré published relativity a year before Einstein and then showed by those theorems that it was false, and that this was why the theory was carried elsewhere.
He gave his own experience as evidence of the cost. He had held the highest-paid postdoctoral position in the country at Catholic University, running a National Science Foundation grant to treat a thousand inoperable brain tumours with negative pion beams made at Los Alamos — the pion stopping in the brain, replacing an electron, entering the nucleus and breaking it up — with 990 of the thousand tumours destroyed and no notable side effects; and he was dismissed by the NSF and the Department of Energy after giving a paper to the American Physical Society arguing that logic falsifies special and general relativity. Scott A. Mainwaring is an American consultant and philanthropist based in Helena, Montana, who is known within Electric Universe circles as a principal supporter and co-founder of the SAFIRE Project, an experimental effort to test the Electric Sun model.
Biography
Mainwaring resides in Helena, Montana, where he has worked as a consultant and part-time lecturer. He is the son of Bruce Mainwaring, a longtime advocate of the Electric Universe idea, and together they have directed the Mainwaring Archive Foundation, the philanthropic vehicle through which the family has funded independent scientific research.
Mainwaring became involved in Electric Universe research after attending the 2012 Electric Universe conference, where he encountered the proposal of engineer Montgomery Childs to build an apparatus capable of testing the Electric Sun hypothesis empirically.
Work
Mainwaring recognized in Montgomery Childs' proposal a pragmatic, empirical method for testing the Electric Universe hypothesis, and in particular the Electric Sun model. He introduced the proposal to his father, Bruce Mainwaring, and the two decided to support the initiative through the Mainwaring Archive Foundation.
The resulting effort became the SAFIRE Project, which sought to reproduce and study, in the laboratory, plasma conditions resembling those proposed for the Sun. The project proceeded through a bench-top proof-of-concept phase, a full-scale laboratory phase built around the "SAFIRE Plasma Engine," and subsequent research into the molecular and atomic-scale reactions observed in its plasma environments. Beyond financing the work, Mainwaring consulted regularly with Childs and contributed hands-on assistance during construction of the Phase 2 apparatus.
The SAFIRE Project was later carried forward as a commercial enterprise under Aureon Energy Ltd.

Should Spacetime be Discarded? was a live session presented by Roger J Anderton on 4 May 2024 in the John Chappell Natural Philosophy Society live session series.
There are problems unifying Einstein's relativity with quantum physics as is well-known. One proposal for unifying them is to discard spacetime. Introducing spacetime into modern physics has created many problems.
Summary
Roger J Anderton hosted this himself, continuing from his sessions on Minkowski spacetime. The question is whether adding spacetime to physics was a mistake, and his angle is that the answer is now being given inside the mainstream as well as outside it: one proposal for unifying relativity with quantum theory is to discard spacetime altogether.
His framing is the historical one he uses repeatedly. The 1905 paper contains no spacetime; Minkowski added it in 1908; general relativity followed in 1915; and between those dates the theory turned into something else. He cited Alexander Unzicker as holding that the development went wrong in exactly that decade.

The first was Sabine Hossenfelder on whether gravity is a force, played to set out the position he disputes. Her account: weight is a force and mass a scalar, a distinction that does not matter in daily life; in general relativity there is no force acting on masses at all, only masses navigating a curved spacetime whose curvature we see indirectly as gravity; the equivalence principle makes the effects of gravity locally the same as acceleration in flat space, so that Einstein and Newton differ over the man who jumps off a roof — Newton says gravity pulls him down, Einstein that the force which had been pushing him up has been removed. title: Sloan Digital Sky Survey
content_preview:
The Sloan Digital Sky Survey ( SDSS ) is a long-running imaging and spectroscopic survey of the sky, begun in 2000 and named for the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation, which funded it. It is the source of much of the observational material that arguments about redshift , quasars and large-scale structure have been conducted on for the past twenty-five years — including a number of the arguments recorded on this wiki.
This article is a short account of the survey oriented to that use. It describes what SDSS is and where it now stands, and then sets out the particular data products that pages on this wiki draw on, and what the disputes over them have been.
The survey
SDSS observes with two telescopes: the Sloan Foundation 2.5 m telescope at Apache Point Observatory in New Mexico, which has carried the survey since the beginning, and the du Pont 2.5 m telescope at Las Campanas Observatory in Chile, which extends it to the southern sky.
Its work divides into two kinds. Imaging records the positions, brightnesses and colours of objects; the imaging camera was retired in 2009, by which time the survey had photometered several hundred million objects over roughly a third of the sky. Spectroscopy — now the whole of the survey's activity — measures the spectrum of a selected object, which is what yields a redshift and hence, on the standard interpretation, a distance.
The survey has run in five phases:
SDSS-I (2000–2005) — the original imaging and redshift survey
SDSS-II (2005–2008) — adding a Milky Way structure survey and the Sloan Supernova Survey
SDSS-III (2008–2014) — including BOSS, the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey
SDSS-IV (2014–2020) — extending to the southern hemisphere
SDSS-V (2020– ) — the current phase, organised as three "mappers": the Milky Way Mapper , the Black Hole Mapper (a time-domain spectroscopic survey of quasars and X-ray sources) and the Local Volume Mapper

The Society for the Advancement of Autodynamics (SAA) was founded in 1994 in Southern California by David de Hilster , Dr. Ricardo Carezani , Amnon Meyers and others, with the purpose of advancing the theory of Autodynamics as developed by Carezani. It later had a chapter in the United Kingdom, and it remains the publisher of essentially the whole Autodynamics literature.
Activities
Publishing
The Society produced a book early on but sold only a few copies. Its two substantial titles are Autodynamics: Fundamental Basis for a New Relativistic Mechanics (1998), the first comprehensive statement of the theory, and Autodynamics: Storm in Physics (2005). The 1998 book was the first to be mass-printed, putting copies into the thousands.
Beyond the books, the Society publishes Carezani's papers, derivations and expository notes at autodynamics.org . That collection is indexed at Ricardo L Carezani and grouped by subject at Autodynamics ; it includes the derivations ( Frames Derivation , Galilean Simplification , The Superfluous System ), the decay papers ( Muon Decay and Autodynamics , Pion Decay and Autodynamics , Nucleus-Nucleus Collision , The Compton Effect and Autodynamics ), the gravitational programme ( Universal Gravitation in Autodynamics and its four applications), and the neutrino papers ( Origin of the Neutrino , Super-Kamiokande: Super-Proof for Neutrino Non-existence , Neutrinos at Fermi Lab , SN 1987A and the Neutrino ).
Several members appear as authors or editors across that body of work: Lucy Haye as co-author of the astrophysical papers, de Hilster and Meyers as editors, and Brian F. Hall as editor of the Pioneer paper.
Public advocacy
The Society has twice intervened publicly against the neutrino hypothesis. Abstract
Still more shocking than the metaphysical assumption of some initial singularity, is the constant insistence upon the so-called cosmological principle of "homogeneity" and "isotropy" of the Universe. Observations do contradict this principle. And to me, the inhomogeneous, fractal at least on a certain scale range, of the distribution of matter is in itself an important cosmological fact, hitherto almost neglected. Moreover difficultties as to the applicability of the second principle of thermodynamics, observations of abnormal redshifts, etc., are casting large doubts not only upon the standard cosmological models, but even on the interpretation of the observed redshift as due solely to a universal expansion.
Overview
Pecker's paper is a conference contribution — delivered to a meeting at which Halton Arp , Jayant Narlikar and Geoffrey Burbidge also spoke — setting out, from the standpoint of a senior professional astronomer at the Collège de France, why he had never accepted the Big Bang . It is not a paper proposing an alternative model. It is a catalogue of the assumptions he regards as unearned, arranged as five complaints: the initial singularity, the cosmological principle, the arbitrary selection of "significant" facts, the unexamined application of the second law of thermodynamics to the universe as a whole, and the accumulating evidence of anomalous Redshifts .
His central objection is methodological. The standard model, he argues, rests less on observation than on a demand for simplicity — "the argument of simplicity is a Pythagorician argument, which cannot convince" — and Occam's razor is being used not to prune hypotheses but to forbid them. Space Lattice Theory is a physical model proposed by the American engineer Bruce Nappi in which space is not an empty void but a densely packed, crystal-like lattice filling the universe, and in which everything we call matter consists of movable defects — dislocations — in that lattice .
Nappi presents it as a Grand Unification: a single physical medium from which matter, energy, time, cause and effect, gravity and the electromagnetic and nuclear forces are all derived, rather than a collection of separate fundamental entities and interactions. Its central appeal, in his account, is that the explanations it produces are simple and visualizable — the model borrows directly from the well-understood physics of defects in ordinary solids, where dislocations move, interact, attract and repel through an elastic medium.
The theory is set out in his 244-page monograph Space Lattice Theory (2015) and in the book Introduction to Space Lattice Theory: Elements for a Grand Unification of Physics .
The lattice
In place of empty space, Nappi proposes that the universe is packed with a single kind of small object, which he designates an "Aa" . These pack together into a lattice of face-centred cubic structure, infinite in extent and possessing the simplest possible elasticity — in effect a solid, massive crystalline ether .
Everything else follows from the mechanics of that solid. Matter is not a substance added to space but a topological defect in it; energy propagates as elastic disturbance; forces between particles are the stress fields by which defects in a crystal influence one another. Spacetime curvature is the proposal, central to general relativity , that gravitation is not a force acting between bodies but a property of the geometry through which they move. Mass and energy deform a four-dimensional continuum of space and time; bodies then follow the straightest available paths through that deformed geometry, and what Newton described as an attractive force appears as an artefact of the shape of the arena.
It is the single most disputed idea documented on this wiki. Roughly 184 pages engage with it directly — some 84 papers, 44 scientist biographies and 14 books — and around 450 discuss curvature in some form. That places it above push gravity , tired light and the Casimir effect in the volume of material collected here.
What the standard account claims
Albert Einstein 's field equations relate the curvature of spacetime at a point to the energy and momentum present there. The account is economical: one geometric statement replaces both the gravitational force and the flat background of special relativity, and it has passed every precision test put to it, from the perihelion advance of Mercury and the bending of starlight to the Shapiro delay, gravitational redshift, frame dragging, the orbital decay of binary pulsars and the direct detection of gravitational waves in 2015.
Its critics do not generally dispute those measurements. What they dispute is the interpretation — whether geometry is the cause of gravitation or merely an efficient bookkeeping for it.

Special relativity is the physical theory published by Albert Einstein in 1905 in the paper On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies . It describes the relationship between space and time for observers moving uniformly relative to one another, and it replaced the Galilean transformations of classical mechanics with the Lorentz transformations . In mainstream physics it is regarded as extensively confirmed by experiment.
Special relativity is also the single most-discussed subject on this wiki. It is the keyword of more papers catalogued here than any other concept in physics, and the literature indexed under it — several hundred papers, together with dozens of books — is overwhelmingly critical. The critics are not a single school. They disagree with each other about what is wrong, about what should replace the theory, and about whether anything need replace it at all. What they share is the conviction that the theory's two postulates, its derivation, its treatment of time and simultaneity, or its claimed experimental support will not survive careful examination. This article states the theory briefly and then presents that body of work, author by author and argument by argument.

The speed of light in vacuum, written c , is the most heavily loaded constant in modern physics. It fixes the ratio between mass and energy, sets the scale of the electromagnetic field equations, defines the metre, and — in the form of Einstein's second postulate, that c has the same value in every inertial frame regardless of the motion of the source — supplies the foundation on which special relativity is built. Since the 1983 redefinition of the SI metre, c is no longer measured at all: it is defined as exactly 299,792,458 metres per second, and the metre is derived from it.
The literature collected on this wiki treats almost every part of that account as open. The researchers documented here do not agree with one another — some hold that c is constant but relative to a medium or a field rather than to every observer; some that the two-way speed is constant while the one-way speed is not; some that c varies with gravitational potential, with the medium, or with time; some that the constancy observed in experiments is an artefact of the instruments used to measure it; and a few that the light-speed barrier can be exceeded outright. What they share is the conviction that the second postulate was elevated to a principle before the experimental evidence could bear it, and that the 1983 redefinition has since made the question difficult even to ask, because a discrepant measurement now registers as a wrongly calibrated metre rather than as a physical result.
This article states the orthodox position, then organises the objections found in the archive by the idea at stake rather than by author.

Title Speed of Light in 3-Dimensional Euclidean Space
Read in full Link to paper
Author(s) Nina B Sotina , Nadia Lvov
Keywords relativity , aether
Published 2013
No. of pages 7
Abstract
The speed of light according to the Special Theory of Relativity has the same value C with respect to any inertial frame of reference in 4-dimensional pseudo-Euclidean space. An attempt to build an alternative physical model in 3-dimensional Euclidean space brings up a question: in what frame of reference does light move with the speed C? Series of experiments and mathematical reasoning suggest that: 1) the speed of a photon emitted by an atom equals to C if measured with respect to the atom if the atom is at rest or moving with a constant speed with respect to a 3-dimensional inertial frame of reference; 2) the speed of light acquires the value of a constant C near Earth, Sun and other large masses; the energy of the photon depends on the gravitational potential, 3) light has inertial properties.
Overview
Presented at the 20th Natural Philosophy Alliance conference in 2013, this paper by Nina Sotina and Nadia Lvov asks a question that special relativity dissolves rather than answers: if space is ordinary three-dimensional Euclidean space and time is independent of it, then with respect to what does light travel at c ?
Their answer is a modified emission theory. Light leaves an atom at speed c relative to that atom — Walther Ritz's ballistic hypothesis of 1908 — but does not keep that speed. As it propagates it undergoes what the authors call hidden dynamics : its velocity relaxes toward c in the frame of any large nearby mass, and does so without any loss of energy, the change in speed being compensated by a change in the photon's mass. The relativistic kinematics of Minkowski space is then, on this view, a formalism that gets the right answers by encoding a real dynamical process it does not name.

Stanislav V. Adamenko is a Ukrainian physicist and the founder and scientific director of the Electrodynamics Laboratory "Proton-21" in Kiev, established in 1999.
Work
The laboratory's programme is the pursuit of extreme compression of matter in a small-scale terrestrial apparatus, with the aim of reaching densities approaching those of nuclear matter — conditions Adamenko describes as "stellar" and compares to the interiors of white dwarfs and neutron stars.
The method is a pulsed electron beam of up to a kilojoule, at a few hundred keV and lasting tens of nanoseconds, directed at a solid target a few tens of micrometres across. Adamenko's claim is that this acts as a "coherent driver", initiating a self-organising and self-sustaining collapse of the electron–nucleus plasma, and that the collapse produces a wholesale nuclear rearrangement of part of the target: the synthesis of elements across the whole periodic table, the creation of superheavy nuclei beyond any known element, and the conversion of radioactive nuclei into stable ones. The last of these is presented as a possible route to the treatment of nuclear waste.
The work is set out at length in Controlled Nucleosynthesis: Breakthroughs in Experiment and Theory (Springer, 2007), edited with Vladimir Vysotskii and Andrei Vysotskyy, which collects the laboratory's experimental reports and its theoretical account of the collapse. The programme has been presented mainly at the International Conference on Cold Fusion and Condensed Matter Nuclear Science meetings.
The central experimental claims — in particular the detection of stable nuclei with mass numbers between 250 and 500, and the assertion that a milligram of target material undergoes complete nuclear regeneration in each shot — have not been reproduced elsewhere.

Stanley Jeffers is an English-Canadian experimental physicist, Associate Professor (now retired) in the Department of Physics and Astronomy at York University in Toronto. He is best known in this field not for a theory of his own but for having built the principal international forum in which heterodox interpretations of quantum mechanics are argued: he was the executive local organiser of the Vigier Symposia , and co-editor of the volumes that came out of them.
His position is an unusual one among the figures documented on this wiki, and worth stating plainly. Jeffers is a conventionally credentialed experimentalist who has taken heterodox claims seriously enough to organise conferences around them, edit their proceedings, and in several cases test them in the laboratory — while frequently reporting results that do not support the claim in question. He is at once a builder of the dissenting community's institutions and one of its more exacting critics.
Education and career
Jeffers took his B.Sc. in Physics with Special Honours (A.R.C.S.) at Imperial College, University of London, in 1963, and his Ph.D. (D.I.C.) in opto-electronics at the same institution in 1968. content_preview:
Title Static Test for a Gravitational Force Coupled to Type II YBCO Superconductors
Author(s) Ning Li , Glen A Robertson
Keywords gravitational, force, magnetic field, Acceleration, density
Published 1997
Volume Physica. C. Superconductivity,
No. of pages 8
Pages 260-267
Abstract
As a Bose condensate, superconductors provide novel conditions for revisiting previously proposed couplings between electromagnetism and gravity. Strong variations in Cooper pair density, large conductivity and low magnetic permeability define superconductive and degenerate condensates without the traditional density limits imposed by the Fermi energy (??10−6 g cm 3 ). Recent experiments have reported anomalous weight loss for a test mass suspended above a rotating type II, YBCO superconductor, with the percentage change (0.05-2.1%) independent of the test mass' chemical composition and diamagnetic properties. A variation of 5 parts per 104 was reported above a stationary (non-rotating) superconductor. In experiments using a sensitive gravimeter, bulk YBCO superconductors were stably levitated in a DC magnetic field. Changes in acceleration were measured to be less than 2 parts in 108 of the normal gravitational acceleration. This result puts new limits on the strength and range of the proposed coupling between static superconductors and gravity.

Name Steady State Theory
Type Cosmological model
Author(s) Hermann Bondi, Thomas Gold and Fred Hoyle (1948)
Keywords perfect cosmological principle, continuous creation, Big Bang , quasi-steady state , eternal universe
Year 1948
Steady state theory is the cosmological model in which the universe has no beginning and no end, presenting on the large scale the same appearance at every epoch, with new matter created continuously to keep the mean density constant as the universe expands.
The standard account
The theory was put forward in 1948 in two papers in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society : one by Hermann Bondi and Thomas Gold , the other, on a different formal basis, by Fred Hoyle . Its governing assumption is the perfect cosmological principle — the universe is homogeneous and isotropic not only in space, as ordinary cosmology assumes, but also in time. There is therefore no privileged epoch, no "early universe," and no origin event.
The model accepted the observed expansion. To keep the perfect cosmological principle in the face of expansion, matter must appear continuously; the required rate is very small, of the order of one hydrogen atom per cubic metre every billion years, far below any rate that could be detected directly. The universe is thus infinitely old, infinitely extended, and always the same in the mean, with galaxies of every age present everywhere at every time.
The steady state model was the principal rival to the evolving hot-origin cosmology through the 1950s and early 1960s. It was Hoyle who gave the rival theory its name, using the phrase "big bang" dismissively in a 1949 BBC broadcast. The model was falsifiable in a way its rival was not: because it forbids evolution, any evidence that the distant — and therefore earlier — universe differs systematically from the nearby one counts directly against it. Abstract
The phenomenon of stellar collapse is considered from the viewpoint of the neo-Newtonian ballistic theory of light. The restrictions of the special theory of relativity are thus removed. The theory predicts that a collapsing star will expand again, and continue to alternately expand and collapse at a rate depending on the mass and greatest radius of the star. On each cycle material will be lost, including photons which appear to distant observers as the emissions of a pulsar. It is concluded that pulsars are oscillating stars, that these eventually "evaporate" away completely, and that there is no such object as a black hole.
Overview
Waldron's paper, published in Apeiron No. 7 (1990), continues an argument he began in "Do Black Holes Exist?" ( Speculations in Science and Technology , 1983). His original objection was that the gravitational energy released by a collapsing burnt-out star would blow the star apart before it reached the Schwarzschild radius. Correspondence with "a number of leading cosmologists" prompted a rethink, and this paper is the result: instead of an explosion, he now argues for an oscillation . The star collapses, turbulence and rotation halt the infall, it re-expands to nearly its original radius, and the cycle repeats, shedding matter and radiation each time. What a distant observer sees is a pulsar. There is no black hole .
The framework is what Waldron calls the "neo-Newtonian ballistic theory of light" — an emission theory in which Newton's three laws are "inviolable", Einstein's invariance postulate is rejected as "incompatible with the principle of relativity", and light consists of material particles. Stephen Hawking Smoked My Socks: How Beliefs Contaminate Our Opinions — An Astrophysicist's Perspective is a 2014 book by the South African astrophysicist Hilton Ratcliffe , published by the U.S.-based Muse Harbor Publishing in November 2014.
The book asks why a handful of scientists — Stephen Hawking and Albert Einstein foremost among them — become world-famous figures, and argues that their fame has little to do with the substance of their science. Ratcliffe uses this as a starting point to examine how belief shapes and "contaminates" opinion, the tension between belief and instinct in forming a worldview, and what he characterises as the suffocating control that scientific orthodoxy exercises over dissenting ideas. It continues the sceptical, anti-consensus themes of his earlier books The Virtue of Heresy: Confessions of a Dissident Astronomer and The Static Universe: Exploding the Myth of Cosmic Expansion .

Steven B. Bryant is an American researcher and technology executive known for a mathematical critique of the derivations underlying special relativity, and for the alternative framework he calls Modern Mechanics (or Modern Classical Mechanics).
His central technical claim concerns Einstein's Spherical Wave Proof . Bryant argues that the proof establishes only that the transformed coordinates satisfy the general equation of a sphere, not that they lie on the same sphere — and that when the radii are checked, the transformed points turn out to lie on multiple spheres rather than one. Since the purpose of the proof is to establish the relationship between the constancy of the speed of light and the principle of relativity, he concludes that the relationship is not established.
His positive proposal turns on a distinction he says relativity conflates: length versus wavelength . On his account time dilation, length contraction and the twin paradox are all artefacts of using a length-based model to interpret wavelength-based observations, and he reports that equations built on the distinction fit the Michelson-Morley and Ives-Stilwell results substantially more closely than the Einstein-Lorentz equations do.
Bryant was a subject matter leader in the relativity community of the Natural Philosophy Alliance , has spoken at AAAS (American Association for the Advancement of Science) and NPA conferences at universities across the United States, and set out his framework for a general readership in Disruptive: Rewriting the Rules of Physics (2016). A supernova is the catastrophic brightening of a star, in which a single object can for a few weeks outshine the whole galaxy that contains it. Supernovae matter far beyond stellar astrophysics because one class of them, Type Ia , is the standard candle on which the modern distance scale — and with it the claim that cosmic expansion is accelerating — rests.
The standard account
Supernovae are sorted spectroscopically. Core-collapse events (Types II, Ib and Ic) are held to occur when a massive star exhausts its nuclear fuel, its iron core collapses, and the infalling envelope rebounds; most of the released energy escapes as neutrinos. Type Ia events show no hydrogen and are attributed instead to the thermonuclear detonation of a white dwarf that has been driven toward the Chandrasekhar mass of about 1.4 solar masses by accretion from, or merger with, a companion.
The nearest supernova of the modern era, SN 1987A in the Large Magellanic Cloud, was seen on 23 February 1987 and remains the only one for which a neutrino burst was detected. Its expanding, strikingly symmetric triple-ring structure has been imaged for decades.
Type Ia events are treated as standardisable candles: their peak brightness correlates with the decline rate of the light curve, so the shape of the curve is used to correct the peak and yield a distance. In 1998 two teams reported that distant Type Ia supernovae appeared fainter than a freely coasting universe predicts, and this was interpreted as accelerating expansion driven by dark energy . A second argument drawn from the same data is that supernova light curves at redshift z appear stretched by a factor of 1+ z , which is presented as a direct observation of cosmological time dilation .

Supernova observations fit Einstein-deSitter expansion in 4-sphere is a six-page 2004 preprint by Tuomo Suntola and Robert (" Bob ") Day , posted to arXiv as astro-ph/0412701. It is an applied test of Suntola's Dynamic Universe (DU) model against the Type Ia supernova data that underwrote the discovery of accelerating cosmic expansion.
Its claim is narrow and quantitative rather than programmatic: that a one-parameter magnitude–redshift relation derived from a zero-energy balance in a spherically closed, expanding four-dimensional space fits the Riess et al. 2004 supernova compilation at least as well as the two-parameter standard cosmology relation, and does so without dark energy , without accelerating expansion, and without any assumption about Ω m , Ω Λ or the Hubble constant.
Abstract
Recent observations on the redshift and magnitude of distant supernovae have raised fundamental questions of the cosmological structure and the development of space. Interpretation of the observations with the standard cosmology model suggests accelerating expansion of space which requires an assumption of unknown dark energy working against gravitation at cosmological distances. This paper presents an analysis which shows that the observed magnitude redshift relationship is in an excellent agreement with the prediction derived by assuming a zero energy balance of motion and gravitation in an expanding 4-sphere. "Systems in Relative Motion" is a paper by Ricardo L Carezani defending the Autodynamics velocity-sum equation against the objection that it gives visibly wrong answers at everyday speeds. It is written as a running exchange with a physicist who raised that objection, and it is the fullest statement of Carezani's distinction between kinematics and dynamics.
Overview
The Autodynamics velocity sum is
β s u m = 1 − ( 1 − β 1 2 ) ( 1 − β 2 2 ) …
Carezani's correspondent points out that for two velocities of 1 km/h this returns 1.41 km/h rather than 2 km/h, and concludes that Autodynamics is therefore wrong. Carezani concedes the arithmetic without reservation — "You are right. There is no mistake in your calculation" — and answers that the two calculations are about different things.
The argument
Kinematics against dynamics
The distinction Carezani draws is between composing velocities without expending energy (kinematics) and composing them by expending it (dynamics). Classical mechanics gives 2 km/h and special relativity 1.9999 km/h because both are answering a kinematic question; Autodynamics gives 1.41 km/h because it is answering a dynamic one, in which the second increment of velocity has to be paid for out of the moving body's own mass.
His correspondent's rejoinder is the natural one: "in the universe we happen to find ourselves in, if I am traveling at 1 km/hour, and I see someone pass me at 1 km/hour, then a third person on the ground will measure his speed at approximately 2 km/hour … Hence, at least in this case, AD is wrong." Abstract
The second of two papers arguing that the theory of moving charge carriers cannot explain the electrical conduction of the Hall effect . Part II attacks the concept of the positively charged "hole" as a category mistake, and proposes instead that the sign of the Hall coefficient is governed by crystal structure , within a model in which conduction is the propagation of a state of charge distribution rather than a flow of charges.
The argument against holes
Marinsek's target is the standard account in which conduction in a solid is carried by electrons and by holes — vacancies in a filled band treated as particles of effective positive charge. His objection is not quantitative but conceptual, and he states it as a category mistake : "a successive occurrence of different holes is not identical with the movement of one hole." A hole, on his account, is simply the previous location of an electron; a location cannot move unless the atom moves, which the theory does not claim.
He works this through the "row of seats" analogy used in textbook expositions and in the Wikipedia article on the electron hole, in which people shift one seat along and the empty seat appears to travel the other way. The analogy fails, he argues, on the same point: seat #4 does not move towards the edge of the row, and all that occurs is a succession of empty seats.
From this he draws the stronger claim, which is where the ontological objection lies. Treating the absence of an electron as a particle amounts to a transubstantiation of an empty place into a positron — a creation ex nihilo . Title The 1855 Weber-Kohlrausch Experiment (The Speed of Light)
Read in full Link to paper
Author(s) David Tombe
Published 2019
Journal General Science Journal
Abstract
In the year 1855, German physicists Wilhelm Eduard Weber and Rudolf Kohlrausch performed an experiment with a Leyden jar and established the ratio between electrostatic and electrodynamic units of charge. This ratio became known as Weber’s constant and it is numerically equal to c√2, where c is the speed of light. In 1857, another German physicist Gustav Robert Kirchhoff used Weber’s constant to conclude that electric signals travel along a wire at the speed of light. A few years later in 1861, Scottish physicist James Clerk Maxwell was working on the physical medium responsible for magnetic lines of force and he had established a linkage between its transverse elasticity and the ratio of electrostatic to electromagnetic units of charge. Electromagnetic units of charge are related to electrodynamic units by a factor of √2. In order to evaluate this ratio, Maxwell looked up Weber’s results, and on converting Weber’s constant into electromagnetic units, the speed of light was exposed. This paper sets out to establish the fundamental origins of the speed of light.
Overview
Dated 14 April 2019 and posted to the General Science Journal , this paper by David Tombe of Northern Ireland is a historical reconstruction with a thesis attached. Its subject is the experiment Wilhelm Weber and Rudolf Kohlrausch performed in 1855, which measured the ratio between the electrostatic and electrodynamic units of charge and so, unexpectedly, produced a velocity.
Tombe traces what followed: Kirchhoff's use of that ratio in 1857 to conclude that electric signals travel along a wire at the speed of light; and Maxwell's use of it in 1861, while working on the elastic medium responsible for magnetic lines of force, to expose the speed of light directly and connect it to the transverse elasticity of the luminiferous medium.

An asymptote is a goal that can probably never be reached, and if reached, cannot be crossed. If crossed, there may be no return. There are at least six asymptotes that apply to our universe. Robert Heaston's essay is a philosophical argument rather than a calculation — he says explicitly that "no mathematics or equations will be used." Its occasion was the May 2003 Scientific American cover feature announcing that parallel universes "probably real... should exist in four different ways," and his purpose is to argue the opposite case: that our universe is bounded by asymptotes we cannot pass, and that theories which cross them have left physics behind.
He identifies six such bounds and arranges them as the faces of a box. Birth and death form the front and back; the speed of light and the gravitational collapse limit form the two sides; absolute zero is the floor and what he calls the superforce is the ceiling. The pairing is deliberate: birth and death are limits on time, light speed and collapse are limits on space, absolute zero and the superforce are limits on matter, so that the box's structure follows from the three basic units.

The Atom is a 1920 book by Albert Cushing Crehore setting out an alternative to the Bohr model of the atom. It is not an exposition of accepted atomic physics but an argument against the theory that had just become standard, together with a rival theory of Crehore's own — one in which the hydrogen atom has two electrons rather than one, a whole series of spectral lines is emitted in a single operation rather than one line per jump, and gravitation is derived from the motion of the electrons inside atoms .

Why the book was written
Crehore explains in the first pages that he would ordinarily have published this work as a series of papers in the technical journals, as he had done for many years, but that the argument needed more space than a journal would give and that condensing it would weaken rather than strengthen it. He is explicit about what he is doing:

He adds that Bohr's work is "most suggestive, and as marking an epoch in the progress of atomic theory." The dispute is with the theory, not with its author.

Abstract
One of the enduring mysteries of classical and modern physics arises from the fact that the value obtained for the gravitational-mass ratio of two particles compared in a weighing experiment is identical to the value obtained for the inertial-mass ratio of the same two particles compared in a collision experiment (to within experimental error). For this reason we speak of the equivalence between inertial and gravitational mass, and tend to use the concepts interchangeably. However, whilst practitioners of science and engineering have been content to accept this equivalence as a matter of fact, there has, until recently, been no rational understanding of it. However, recently, Ghosh, Assis and I have each given the basis for such an understanding.
Overview
A three-page paper written while David F Roscoe was in the Department of Applied Mathematics at the University of Sheffield, published in Apeiron in June 1992. The Expanding Earth: Some Consequences of Dirac's Gravitation Hypothesis is a 1971 book by the physicist Pascual Jordan , published by Pergamon Press. It is an English translation (by Arthur Beer) of his 1966 German work Die Expansion der Erde (Braunschweig: Friedrich Vieweg).
Overview
Jordan takes up Paul Dirac's "large numbers" hypothesis of a gradual weakening of the gravitational constant G over cosmic time, and works out its geophysical consequences. He argues that, as gravity has weakened, the Earth has slowly expanded — swelling from an initial ball perhaps only about 7,000 km in diameter to its present size — and he connects this to continental drift, the growth of the ocean basins, and other geological evidence. The book is a rare instance of a major theoretical physicist developing the Expanding-Earth idea from a specific cosmological hypothesis.
About the author
Pascual Jordan (1902–1980) was a German theoretical physicist and one of the founders of quantum mechanics and quantum field theory (the Born–Heisenberg–Jordan "three-man paper," and Jordan–Wigner quantization). In his later career he worked on cosmology and gravitation, including scalar-tensor ("Jordan–Brans–Dicke") theories of varying gravity, of which the Expanding Earth was a proposed consequence.

The Farce of Physics is a book by Bryan G Wallace (1933–1997), copyright 1993, arguing that "modern theoretical physics has become to a large degree, little more than an elaborate farce." It is part memoir, part polemic and part sociology of science: an account of Wallace's roughly fifty-year career as a physicist working outside the academic mainstream, organised around his contention that Einstein's second postulate — the constancy of the velocity of light — is contradicted by interplanetary radar data and is the load-bearing assumption of everything built on it.
It was never issued by a publisher. Wallace circulated it over the early internet, and it remains freely readable in full; see Reading the book below.
The central argument
Wallace states the thesis of the book most compactly in Chapter 4, prompted by a reader's question in Marilyn vos Savant's newspaper column about what single discovery would overturn modern science:
Einstein's special relativity theory with his second postulate that the speed of light in space is constant is the linchpin that holds the whole range of modern physics theories together. Shatter this postulate, and modern physics becomes an elaborate farce!
His evidence for shattering it is the one he had pressed since 1969: that published interplanetary radar data, in particular the 1961 radar contact with Venus, fit a classical c + v relative velocity better than a constant c . The book's wider claim is that the physics community's failure to engage with this is not an accident but a symptom — of funding structures, of peer review, and of what he regards as physics having taken on the character of a faith.
The title is a deliberate echo of Fritjof Capra's The Tao of Physics , which Wallace quotes

Summary
Jeff Baugher 's objection to relativity does not concern relativity. It concerns the calculus the theory was built on — and, he argued, a confusion in the notation that has stood unresolved for four hundred years. He does not mention Einstein anywhere in the presentation, because his argument is with the mathematics Einstein was taught rather than with what Einstein made of it.

"The Holor Representation of Polarization" is a 1994 paper by Domina Eberle Spencer , Uma Y Shama and Terri L Mascardo , published in the Journal of the Illuminating Engineering Society . It applies the algebra of holors to the description of the polarization of light.
Overview
A holor is a mathematical object made up of one or more independent components (called merates ), introduced by Parry Moon and Domina Eberle Spencer in their book Theory of Holors (Cambridge University Press, 1986). The holor concept was proposed as a generalization broad enough to embrace scalars, vectors, matrices, tensors and other multi-component quantities within a single formalism, with a common index notation and a general account of how the components transform. The motivation is that many quantities useful in physics are not tensors, even though the tensor calculus is often treated as the only rigorous framework; holor algebra is offered as a way of handling that wider class of entities on the same footing.
In this paper the authors turn that framework on polarization — the orientation of the transverse oscillations of a light wave. Polarized light is conventionally described in several separate ways: by the two-component complex Jones vector, by the four real Stokes parameters, and by the Mueller matrices that transform them as light passes through optical elements. The paper recasts these descriptions within the holor formalism, giving a unified holor representation of the polarization state and of the operations that act on it. It belongs to a series of works in which Spencer and Moon extended holor methods into physical optics and photometry, the field in which much of their joint work appeared.

Abstract
"For any speculation which does not at first glance appear crazy, there is no hope." F. Dyson. To understand the process that brings about the effects of gravitation we must change profoundly the way we perceive the world. We must discard the idea of an invisible "field" that causes gravitation and develop in its place the concept of a direct mechanical effect produced by a hydrodynamic ether. The key intellectual shift involves understanding that the omnipresent ether manifests equally well as open space or as material bodies. Thus objects cease to be separate entities and become local manifestations of the ether. The universal etheric context is always in motion and has a velocity gradient - dv/dr - at every point. It is the direction and magnitude of the etheric velocity gradient that determines the direction and strength of gravitational effects. This perceptual shift is as difficult and counterintuitive as the shift from the Ptolemaic to the Copernican view. Once mastered, it brings the same clarification to gravitational effects that Copernicus brought to the motions of heavenly bodies.

The Hundred Year Detour is a seven-page essay by Jerry Shifman , dated March 2006 and presented at the 15th Natural Philosophy Alliance Conference in 2008. It is an argument in prose rather than mathematics; there are no equations and no data.

The intellectual shift required, Shifman argues, is to see that "the omnipresent ether manifests equally well as open space or as material bodies", so that objects are not separate things but local features of one medium — a change he compares to the move from Ptolemy to Copernicus.

University physics courses teach that centrifugal force doesn’t exist, while university applied maths courses teach that centrifugal force is merely a fictitious force that arises when making observations from a rotating frame of reference.
